TEMPLEMAN (Minister ot Inland Revenue) moved for leave to introduce a Bill (No. 127) respecting Commercial Feeding Stuffs. He said: This Bill proposes to deal with feeding stuffs for domestic animals. There is no law dealing with these substances other than indirectly. The Bill runs pretty much along the line of another Bill now on the Order

Paper dealing with agriculture fertilizers. It is proposed to compel manufacturers of commercial feeding stuffs to register and sell their products under a number given by the Inland Revenue Department, and to put upon the packages the guaranteed analyses of the contents of the food sold, thus creating to some extent, a standard by which the manufacturers of these foodstuffs will sell and affording the purchaser some guarantee of the genuineness of the article bought. The Bill is believed to be very much in the interests of the purchaser and has been approved by agricultural associations and others interested.

Do I understand that other cattle foods than bran or shorts must have branded on the package the contents showing exactly what the mixture is made of? Farmers complain that when they buy bran, instead of getting pure bran, sweepings and other stuff are mixed with it, so that the purchaser does not know what he is buying.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
The Bill covers the point raised by the hon. member. It relates to any article offered for sale for the feeding of domestic animals, including those claimed to possess medicinal as well as nutritive properties. Hay, straw, roots, the ordinary meals of wheat, rye, barley, oats or corn, and also bran or middlings of any of these grains sold separately, must be genuinely what they profess to be, and must not be mixed.
Motion agreed to and Bill read the first time.

I desire to bring a matter before the attention of the House. On the 17th of February I asked for a return of the amount that was paid to the Logberg Printing Company. On the 26th of March that return was brought down, stating that the amount was some $500, for the Public Works Department only. All other departments return report nil. In looking over the Auditor General's Report I find that for the year 1908 alone there was a sum of $4,752 paid to this company. I wish to call attention to a matter which refers to the departments of the Minister of Labour and the Minister of Railways and Canals. I have here a report sent to me from Prince, a Prince Rupert paper, based upon the telegram from Vancouver.
Vancouver, March 27.-Royal mail steamer ' Monfceagle ' arrived from the orient yesterday with sixty Russian moujiks from Siberia, imported to work on the Grand Trunk Pacific construction from Prince Rupert east. The moujiks are to replace the Englishspeaking labourers, who do not really conform to hard conditions and to the wages they have been receiving. The Russians are to work in a colony bv themselves, just as Italian gangs do, if they prove satisfactory. They are to be taken to Prince Rupert on the 'Princess May.' It is not learned what they are to be paid; but it is evident they are under something like the padrone system. Another and larger party is to arrive on the next Canadian Pacific Railway steamer.
If this despatch represents the true condition of affairs, it shows that contract labour of a very degraded kind is being imported for service on the Grand Trunk Pacific. On another page of (the same paper there is an article setting forth that a year ago the firm of Foley, Welch and Stewart, of St. Paul, Minnesota, of Spokane Washington, and of Winnipeg, Manitoba, entered into a contract to grade 100 miles of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway beginning at Prince Rupert. The Prince Rupert ' Empire ' states that they had 2,500 men at work a month ago, but that the work was going on very slow, and it gives as a reason that the sub-contractors were employing labour of an inferior quality. The ' Empire ' goes on to say:
Foley, Welch & Stewart, as practical railway builders, have a system of carrying on their business. The system is a 'good one for Foley, Welch & Stewart, however poor it may be for the men who do the work. They will not change it, no matter if men injured on the work are treated worse than brutes are treated on farm? in Ontario; no matter if men who earn wages are put to undue expense to collect the wages earned; no matter if the subcontractors, who are judgment proof, cause loss to station men; no matter if expensive plant remains idle for weeks at a time owing to petty disputes over wages. They know that the Dominion government moves slowly, if it moves at all.

I will proceed then to present the facts in this way:	Section
40 of the National Transcontinental Railway Act, chapter 71, 1903, provides that:
The company shall, before being entitled to the guarantee provided by this agreement, furnish evidence, satisfactory to the government, that all just claims of contractors and for materials, wages and supplies, and all just claims against contractors and sub-contractors for materials, wages and supplies, entering into and supplied for the construction of the railway have been duly paid.

Mr. Speaker, I desire to crave your indulgence and that of the the House for a very brief personal explanation. The explanation refers to a paragraph which appears in a newspaper called the 'Toronto Sunday World.' In that paragraph the writer purports to give an account of the proceedings in this House last Friday evening and in that report he uses these words:
Mr. Stanfield, the husky member for Colchester, overheard the member from Red Deer apply an insulting epithet to Mr. Foster. He warned Dr. Clark that if he did not instantly withdraw he would thrash him; and after looking Mr. Stanfield carefully over, the apology was forthcoming.
Mr. Speaker, during the time that I have had the honour of knowing the hon. member for Colchester, I wish to ask you, Sir, and this House, to believe me when I state that he has never addressed to me one single word which, interpreted according to the strictest canons, could be called ungentlemanly or impolite, much less has he ever used to me language which, by any stretch of the imagination, could be called threatening. I wish the House to believe this further statement that there was no language of this description used towards me; so that there was no withdrawal or apology forthcoming from me. I regret to have to call attention to this incident at all, because I may say that I have carefully read a large number of the newspaper accounts of what happened 124}

on Friday night and these accounts are very generally truthful, very generally unexaggerated and reflect the very greatest credit upon the press of this country. In 'regard to the paragraph to which I have just referred and to which I wish to give the most emphatic contradiction, I can only say, in quoting the language of Macaulay in regard to certain scribes of his day, that the people who compose these paragraphs 'act after their kind.'

Mr. Speaker, I would like to draw the attention of the House to the fact that there is another member of this House who has been maligned to some extent by the same article in this edition of the 'Toronto Sunday World.' A little farther on this article proceeds to say:
Later in the House Mr. Stanfield got into a heated argument with Mr. Neely, of Humboldt and threatened that member with extermination if he did not withdraw a remark, also applied to Mr. Foster. The affair was patched up by friends.
I want to say, Sir, that I am sorry the hon. member for Colchester (Mr. Stanfield) is not here to-day, because I am sure that he would give to this quite as emphatic a denial as my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark) has to the paragraph just preceding. The hon. member for Colchester could not possibly have had any excuse or reason for threatening to exterminate me on account of any statements or epithets applied to the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) because I did not apply any epithets to that hon. gentleman. I did not say anything to the hon. gentleman for North Toronto, either agreeable or disagreeable, unless it might be something in the way of mild admonition that he should take his medicine in common with remarks of that kind applied by quite a number of the members of this House.
House in committee on Bill (No. 81) respecting the Manitoba and North Western Railway Company of Canada.-Mr. Cash.

When this Bill was before the committee on Friday last, Mr. Chairman, I placed in your hands an amendment. I would point out that paragraph A of section 9, of chapter 52, of the statutes of 1893, refers to that part of the charter of this company granted in 1893 for the building of a branch line from the town of York-ton to the city of Prince Albert in the present province of Saskatchewan. The effect of my amendment, if it is carried, is to strike out the particular paragraph in the Bill now before the committee, which has reference to the building of the branch line from Yorkton to the city of Prince Albert.

The reason I have brought this matter before the committee is, that this Manitoba and Northwestern charter has had a very striking history; a histroy which if thoroughly known to the members of the House would not I am sure inspire in them any feelings of sympathy towards that charter. I have had very strong representations from the people in that part of the country protesting against the renewal of this charter. The Canadian Pacific Railway have held the Manitoba and Northwestern charter, as the House knows, since 1893 or practically for sixteen years, and the charter was in existence for some twelve or thirteen years previous to that. Therefore, the charter for this particular line of railroad that I am referring to has been in existence practically since the year 1880, the year in which the original Manitoba and Northwestern charter was passed by the Manitoba legislature. The Canadian Pacific Railway therefore have held this charter for sixteen years, and while they have made surveys two or three times, and while they have gathered together a few shovels full of earth in the shape of starting to grade at one or two points along the proposed line, they have practically made no use whatever of this particular charter. I want the committee to understand that this has been a very great hardship to a great many peo-pie who have gone into this section on the understanding and with the expectation that the Canadian Pacific Railway had taken over the charter in good faith for the purpose of building this piece of road. Every means possible have been taken to bring pressure to bear upon the Canadian Pacific Railway to construct this piece of road. For instance, in looking up chapter 52 of the statutes of 1893, I find that section 9 gives the power to build these particular lines of railroad, and subsection 3 of that section provides:
The company shall construct and complete to the satisfaction of the Governor in Council, not less than 20 miles of railway on or before the 31st day of December in each calendar year after the year 1893, or otherwise their powers under this section shall cease as regards so much of the said lines of railway as is not completed by the said date in each calendar year.
That means that there has been a provision in this charter ever since the Cnnadian Pacific Railway have taken it over, as there was before that time, to the effect that this company was to build twenty miles every year. To show what attention they have paid to this provision, I may mention that they have not built one single mile of line from the town of Yorkton to the city of Prince Albert. Then again, I object to the way in which the Canadian Pacific Railway undertake to get their extensions of time for these charters so long over due. I object to the way in which they undertake to get such legislation through the Railway Mr. NEELY.
Committee and through this House. In this Bill (No. 81) which is before us ait present, they are asking for an extension of time on some other branch lines, the charters for which they have obtained since 1893. In or der to cover up the fact that they have held the charter for this particular branch line for the past sixteen years they run in three or four other charters which have been granted in more recent times. This particular charter that we are considering illustrates very well the futility of putting in any requirements as to building a road in the case of the Canadian Pacific Railway; because as I say there is this provision in the charter ever since they took it over, and for that matter before they took it over, to the effect that they must build twenty miles every calendar year. The fact of the matter is that they have never carried out that condition, but they apparently find it easier to come back to parliament to obtain a renewal of the charter. Now, Sir, I think that sixteen years is a reasonable length of time in which to have allowed the Canadian Pacific Railway to accomplish something on this road.
Twenty-nine years.

Twenty-nine years so far as the whole charter is concerned, but the Canadian Pacific Railway have held it since 1893 or for sixteen years. I think something should be done now, and I would like the promoter of the Bill to tell this committee, what he did not tell the Railway Committee, why it is that the Canadian Pacific Railway are asking to have this charter renewed. It is only a couple of weeks ago that in Bill (No. 79) the Canadian Pacific Railway obtained from this House an extension of time for the construction of the branch line from the town of Lanigan on the Kirkella branch up to the city of Prince Albert. I am sure the hon. gentleman who is promoting this Bill has no confidence in his own mind that the Canadian Pacific Railway intends to build this particular piece of road, or at all events that it intends to build it in the immediate future. Why should this House grant this renewal of time when we have no evidence whatever that the Canadian Pacific Railway intend to build. If they did intend to build they should at least say so, and yet I have it on good authority that this branch line is not part of their programme for this next year, and so far as I can obtain any information it is not a part of their programme for the year following. The people in that part of the country do not want this extension granted. Their view is that if this charter is not renewed that probably some local capitalists or promoters may become interested in building a railway from Prince Albert to some point on the main line of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway.

Whether they are Tight or wrong the people of that part of the country feel that the granting of a charter to the Canadian Pacific Railway tends to prevent other railroads from seeking for charters through the same territory. I am strongly of the same opinion. We know perfectly well that in a great many cases the obtaining of a charter by promoters who are not actual railroad builders does not prevent others from obtaining charters and constructing railroads; but in the case of the Canadian Pacific Railway it is an entirely different proposition because so long as that road holds a charter for a certain territory and the section will support only one line, no other railroad company will undertake to get a charter through that territory, and if another railroad company should obtain a charter and begin building the Canadian Pacific Railway would immediately get busy in order to stop the construction of the competing line of Tailroad. That is the policy of the Canadian Pacific Railway, and I am convinced in my own mind that that is the only reason why they are seeking an extension of time for this particular charter, in order to blanket this territory and keep any other railroad from undertaking to build through it. So I think the view of the people of that part of the country is reasonable, and that unless the Canadian Pacific Railway immediately commence construction the charter should be taken away from them. It is merely a question of asking the Canadian Pacific Railway to quit playing dog in the manger. I am not finding any fault with the operation of the Canadian Pacific Railway. The argument most frequently advanced in favour of granting such extensions of time to the Canadian Pacific Railway is that they have such an extensive programme of railway construction in the west. I do not think that is any excuse for the Canadian Pacific Railway not building this particular line. Whv should the Canadian Pacific Railway not have an extensive programme of building branch lines and other lines in the Canadian Northwest? I would like to know whether the people of the Canadian Northwest are under any compliment to the Canadian Pacific Railway for the amount of railway construction they are carrying on there. The wealth of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company has been obtained to a very large extent from the resources of the Canadian Northwest, and the people of that country do not feel under any compliment to the Canadian Pacific Railway for the building of their branch lines. They are using the people's money, they are using the resources of western Canada, which were given to them by the terms of their original contract That argument I say, therefore, does not hold water, because we feel that we are entitled to all the railroad construction we are getting from
the Canadian Pacific Railroad. Whether this amendment of mine carries or not, I shall continue so long as I am a member of this House to use every legitimate means I possess to prevent these extensions of time to the Canadian Pacific Railway or any other company unless the company is in a position to give some reasonable excuse or reason for not having carried out the terms of its charter, I shall oppose the granting of any extensions which will enable a company to blanket territory for no other purpose than to keep .other railroads from building through it.

Mr. Speaker, I shall not discuss the mode of construction of railways by the Canadian Pacific Railway in the west. I assume that hon. members fully appreciate what the Canadian Pacific Railway has done and what they are endeavouring to do, but I must say that I think it is a mistake to depreciate, as some hon. members have done, what that great railway corporation are and have been doing. I do not believe in throwing obstacles in their way if they are endeavouring to give railway accommodation to the people in the west. The whole matter lies in a nutshell. In 1903 the Manitoba and Northwestern Railway Company applied for and obtained a charter to construct a railway from Yorkton in a northwesterly direction to Prince Albert on the north branch of the Saskatchewan river. The sub-clause of section 9 now in question reads:
The company may lay out, construct and operate the following lines of railway of the gau^e of 4 feet Si inches.
(a) An extension of the main line from the present terminus' at Yorkton in a northwesterly direction to a point at or near Prince Albert on the north branch of the Saskatchewan river.
The hon. member's amendment repeals this subsection which would have the effect of repealing the right to construct a railway, repealing a charter which gave the Manitoba and Northwestern Railway Company the power to construct a railway from Yorkton to Prince Albert. The hon. gentleman forgets or perhaps he is not familiar with the territory. I do not claim to be very familiar with it; I have been in Yorkton but I was never beyond Yorkton on that road, but I understand distinctly from my hon. friend from McKenzie, that the Canadian Pacific Railway or the Manitoba and Northwestern Company, whichever it is, has already constructed nearly 50 miles of that road and that it is in operation today. I spoke to a gentleman to-day who told me he had travelled over that road, that it is in actual operation; yet here is an attempt on the part of an hon. gentleman from the west to repeal an Act of parliament which authorizes the construction' of a road of which nearly 50 miles has been

built and is now in operation. I submit to the House that such a thing was never attempted in parliament, and although parliament has the power to do almost anything it would be interfering with the right of that railway company in reference to an undertaking which it is now carrying on that I do not think this parliament would for a moment tolerate.

I would say to the hon. member that his statement that 50 miles had been built on the line from "Yorkton to Prince Albert is absolutely contrary to the facts of the ease.
An. hon. MEMBER. How many miles?
None whatever.
I think there are men in the House who know that territory better than the hon. gentleman does.
I know the country very well.
The hon. member from Huron told me he had travelled over that road.
So I did, from Yorkton to Sheho.

I am satisfied that the hon. gentleman who is promoting this Bill (Mr. Cash) is familiar with the fact that that portion of the road has been constructed from Yorkton to Sheho, a distance of 40 or 50 miles, sufficient to warrant this House in defending the charter of the company which constructed that road. My hon. friend seems to be entirely mistaken. He will find on inquiry that he is attempting to repeal the charter of a road, a considerable portion of which has already been constructed. The Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) is not in his place but I am sure the right hon. the Prime Minister will not consent that, where a charter has been granted and the company has constructed such a large portion of the road, that the charter will be taken from the company. The charter was obtained in 1893. In 1902 the time was extended for the construction of the line mentioned in subsections A and B. In 1907 it was extended for the completion of the railway authorized by section 9 of chapter 52. Not only have these charters been kept alive by parliament, but the company has gone ahead in good faith and constructed nearly 50 miles of road. That surely entitles them to the consideration of the House, and I do not think that, under the circumstances, the House will repeal the very charter under which the company are now operating the railway to that extent. I submit that my hon. friend must be labouring under a serious mistake or he would not have introduced this amendment.

The hon. gentleman is entirely wrong and so is the hon. member for East Huron (Mr. Chisholm). The line of railway from Yorkton to Sheho has nothing to do with the line from Yorkton to Prince Albert. That is a line going westward and which will connect with the Kirk-ella at the town of Lanigan.
I do not understand it in that way. I travelled over that road before the extension was made to Lanigan, and I understood it was part of this very road to Prince Albert.
I think that the hon. gentleman who is promoting the Bill will say that the line from Yorkton to Sheho is being extended to Lanigan and is almost completed at present.

The clause of the Act of 1893, which it is sought to repeal, is the clause that authorizes the construction of a road from Yorkton to Prince Albert. I am not speaking of the road from Sheho westerly as that is a different charter altogether. The language is unmistakable that this is a charter for a road now in operation, and I cannot see how the hon. member for Humboldt can fail to be mistaken. The section says:
Extension of the main line from the present terminus at Yorkton in a northwesterly direction to a point at or near Prince Albert on the Saskatchewan river.
There is no other railway running from Yorkton in that direction to Sheho. The road from Sheho to which the hon. gentleman has referred is another charter running westward from Sheho to a place called Lanigan, but the hon. gentleman has made a mistake. He is repealing too much. If he had submitted an amendment to repeal a portion of subsection A in section 9 of the Act of 1893-that portion lying between Sheho and Prince Albert, he might have had some ground for his appeal; but he is asking the House to repeal the entire charter from Yorkton to Prince Albert or the road running from Yorkton, through Sheho and on to Prince Albert. The hon. member for McKenzie (Mr. Cash) will substantiate what I have said with reference to the portion of the road constructed and now in operation.

I am perfectly familiar with the conditions. The road runs from Portage La Prairie with a terminal at Yorkton. The line extended to Prince Albert under the old survey; and the line built from Yorkton to Sheho is on that old Manitoba and northwestern survey, right in a section where fault was found with the Canadian Pacific Railway for not building the road, many settlers having gone there from Dakota under the conviction that that line

would be built. The line remained at York-ton quite a number of years, but since 1903 it has been extended, on the old survey to Prince Albert, as far as Sheho. After it arrived at Sheho, for some reasons known best to the Canadian Pacific Railway, they went westward to join with their Kirkella branch at a place called Lanigan. They have graded that line and have built to about half way between Sheho and Lanigan and what they are asking now is to go on the old survey from Sheho to Prince Albert. I presume they want to build that road, and I am anxious they should because it will give my section of country the shortest route possible to Prince Albert, and from Prince Albert to Winnipeg. I think that this extension of time should be granted for several reasons. I have no particular interest in the line, but it is of considerable importance to the people in my section of the country that it should be built. The Bill was handed to me to take charge of, and I did so as I was interested in the Manitoba and Northwestern to this extent. I can see the advantage the road will be to my section of the country and to Prince Albert and the country through which it will pass. The people are complaining at not having got the road sooner, and I do not know how they will get it any sooner if we refuse this extension. The Canadian Pacific Railway will probably build the line this summer. I have no doubt that, with the force of men they have on hand, they will begin construction to Prince Albert possibly this fall; but I am not stating this on the authority of the Canadian Pacific Railway people but simply on my own judgment. In my opinion it is their interest to do so as it is the shortest line to Prince Albert and the best. I think the amendment is a great mistake and consequently ought not to be considered. I do not find that the amendment as read by you, Mr. Chairman, agrees with the notice m the Votes and Proceedings.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: There were two amendments proposed. If the hon. gentleman will look at some other copy of the Votes and Proceedings, he will see that the amendment as now put is properly put.

I have the second amendment before me and also the other. The amendment in Friday's Votes and Proceedings reads:
That clause 1 be amended to read as follows: Paragraph A, of section 9, of chapter 52, of the statutes of 1893, is hereby repealed.
There is no question of the clause reading *as clause No. 2.
That would practically cut out the whole of the clause and all the branch lines connected therewith. If clause No. 1 were repealed it would practically cut out the whole of the line, and all the branch lines connected therewith.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

speechtext: I think that ought to be stated in the notice.

As a portion of this line runs through my constituency I wish to support the protest of the hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Neely). The people who live in that section have grave doubts of the intention of the Canadian Pacific Railway to. extend this line to Prince Albert. After sixteen years of promises by the company the people there feel that it is now about time that something should be done. They have been promised this road for many years. People came into that section of the country with the expectation that this road would be built, and they went through many of the hardships of pioneers. They lived from 40 to 80 miles from a railroad. When the Can-dian Pacific Railway acquired the Manitoba and Northwestern road there was a clause in the agreement that they should build 30 miles of this road each year until it was all built. The people thought that it would be done, but they were disappointed. In 1903 they, the people, were given to understand that the company would build their road west to parallel with the Canadian Northern. In 1902, when the Canadian Northern were extending their lines from the boundary of Manitoba west to Prince Albert, the Canadian Pacific Railway did become active for a little while. They put forth considerable effort and ran two surveys, and they	got all their friends	to talk	forthem and	help	them	make the	people	believe that	they	were	going to	Prince	Albert, that	they	were	going on	at once	to
build that road following the surveys. However, nothing was done. They ran their survey lines, and as the Canadian Northern did not stop, they dropped the project and at once turned their road west to parallel the Canadian Northern main line. The people who live in that section of the country and who have undergone great hardships in pioneering felt

very much disappointed. They have been obliged to haul their grain to market, as I said, all the way from 40 to 80 miles. It took them a week to make a trip to Prince Albert, and their expenses about ate up whatever they received for their produce. As this road has turned west and the company has not. yet manifested any intention of building, I think the people have a right to doubt their intention to go on and build this road. No doubt ultimately they will build it, because the growth of the country and its products will sometime or other induce them to construct it. But the people want it now. We know that if another charter was granted to run over this line, no matter to whom it was granted, the Canadian Pacific Railway, being a very powerful company, could in 48 hours put on enough men to start construction, and in this way prevent the other company from going on. There is another reason why we doubt their sincerity. They have not selected any land in the north part of Saskatchewan, their lands are all else where, as are the rest of their interests, and we think they are holding this charter as a blanket. Further than that, this great road in the last eight or ten years has done nothing to promote immigration into our country. When people come up from the States with the intention of going to Prince Albert and other northern points, the company carries them elsewhere, gives them transportation clear out to Calgary in another province entirely. The Canadian Pacific Railway was willing to undertake their transportation and send them on further west rather than allow them to go to the northern parts. Therefore, I say we have certainly reason to doubt their sincerity. We think it is now about time that they should get out and allow us to give a charter to some other company who will be willing to help us develop our section of the country.
I shall support the amendment to the hon. member for Humboldt.
How would the repealing of this charter facilitate you in getting your railroad built?
If this charter was out of the way we could get a new one. But as long as the Canadian Pacific holds the charter they can go to work at any time and start construction and head off any other project.

When this matter was before the Railway Committee I supported the contention of the hon. member for Humboldt. I quite agree that the Canadian Pacific Railway has done a great deal of work in that country, and is doing a great deal of work, and everybody Mr. RUTAN.	.
gives them credit for what they are doing. But it seems to me the fact they are building a certain number of roads is no argument why a charter should be renewed year after year when nothing is being done on that particular charter, and especially when it is a charter that has been in existence for the last 29 years, for the last 16 of which the Canadian Pacific Railway has held it. The Canadian Pacific Railway has had all consideration; but don't you think there ought to be some consideration shown to the settlers in that part of the country? What is the position ? The hon. member for Humboldt and the hon. member for Prince Albert came before the Railway Committee representing those people, and stated that the people in those sections where this line is to run are against the renewal of that charter, simply because, as I have been told, the Canadian Pacific Railway have stated that they have no intention of doing anything on that charter this year.
They have no intention of building for the next two years. Why should not the charter be cancelled so that somebody else may be given an opportunity to come in and build the road, especially when the people of that part of the country ask that that should be done? It comes to this: Are the wishes of the people of the section affected to have any weight with the members of this House, or are the wishes of the Canadian Pacific Railway, who want the charter kept in force and have no intention of building at the present time, to have weight? I, for one, am going to take the ground that the voice of the people should be heard and not the voice of the railways. We do not want to oppose the Canadian Pacific Railway wherever they want to build, but they have had this charter sixteen years and have no intention of building now. There is a misapprehension between the hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Neely) and the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Cash). The road is already built from Yorkton to Sheho. I am not prepared to say whether that was built under the original Manitoba, Northwestern charter, or whether it was built under the new charter the Canadian Pacific Railway has got. But this I am certain of-they got a charter from Sheho, not in a northwesterly direction, but rather in a southwesterly direction to Lanigan, and from Lanigan they got a charter this session to extend through to Prince Albert. This is the second charter they want to get-this being a renewal-from Sheho to Prince Albert. The hon. member from Humboldt (Mr. Neely) is not to blame, for he is taking the language of a former Act of parliament. But what he wants to have cancelled is not the line from Yorkton to

Prince Albert, but the line from Sheho to Prince Albert.
But does not the hon. member (Mr. Turriff) say that the effect of the motion is the opposite of what he says is intended?

There may be something in that. The amendment may not be properly worded. But this branch comes up in connection with five or six others, making it almost impossible to cut out one without cutting out all. But the voice of the people should be heard, and they do not want this charter revived or given any longer existence, for they want to give somebody else an opportunity to go in and build the road.

Will the hon. member allow iqe to ask a question? I want to find out for myself, if I can, what would be the effect of passing this resolution. As I understand it, the Canadian Pacific Railway now can build from Sheho to Prince Albert.
Via Lanigan-they have that charter now.
They have a charter from Sheho to Prince Albert.
That is what they are asking.
Is this by a new charter or by renewal?
By renewal.
They have had, and if this passes they wall continue to have?
They have a charter from Lanigan to Prince Albert.
Each of these charters running through Sheho?
Yes.
Very, well; then they have a charter to run from Lanigan
From Sheho to Lanigan and Lanigan to Prince Albert.
That is, if they get this they wi'l have the right to build two roads to Prince Albert?
Yes.
Suppose the amendment were to pass, what will they have?
They have the road built to Sheho, and they have it built half way from Sheho to Lanigan. They will have the right to continue from Lanigan to Prince Albert.
And cut the people out from Sheho to Prince Albert. What do they say?	.!	1
Nine-tenths of the people from Sheho to Prince Albert say that this has been in existence for sixteen years, and nothing has been done with the charter and so they ask that it be cancelled.
How will that help them?

It will let somebody else come in and build. They have no hope or faith that the Canadian Pacific Railway will build the road. This charter has been in existence for twenty-nine years, and the Canadian Pacific Railway have had it for sixteen years. As the people have no hope that the Canadian Pacific Railway will build, they ask that somebody else be given a chance to do so. They a* suffering, and they are the people whose voice should be heard, and not the voice of the railway company. That is what it comes down to. Let the people themselves judge whether they want the charter or not; they are the ones who will suffer, if, by cancelling this charter, the road is not built. And they ask that that be done. For once, let us do what the people along the line ask should be done.

If we do what the hon, member (Air. Turriff) asks the House to do, the result would be absolutely absurd It would Tepeal the charter under which a road has been built, and is being operated.
Air. TURRIFF I stated that there was a mix-up, and that all that was wanted was to cancel the motion as relating to that part from Sheho to Prince Albert, but not the whole line from Yorkton to Prince Albert.

That is not the amendment. Its effect would be to cancel the whole line. I see by the Canadian Pacific Railway report that a portion of the line has been built. The Alanitoba North Western from Portage la Prairie to Yorkton, 229-9 miles has been built. From Yorkton to. Sheho, 42-2 miles, has been built. If this amendment passes, it would repeal the Act which gave authority to build that line and run it. The hon. member must see how absurd this amendment would be if carried. I see it stated here also that the line from Sheho to Lanigan is under construction, 82-8 miles. Part of the road has been built and running for years, and we are asked to repeal the law under which it is operated. It must be obvious that that is something that cannot be entertained.
It is an easy matter to change the wording to make it apply only to that portion of the line for which they are asking a renewal, from Sheho to Prince Albert.

The hon. member (Mr. Turriff) has spoken of the people wishing to have this charter not renewed. Have the people petitioned this House to that

effect? Another question: Is there a bunch ol capitalists standing by Teady to build this road if the Canadian Pacific Railway loses this charter? These are important questions. It is all right enough to make a great talk before the committee for the benefit of the people, to talk about ' the wishes of the people,' and so on, but the fact remains that no independent company, no company outside the Canadian Northern, the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Grand Trunk Pacific has built ten miles of road in that western country in the last ten years. If the big concerns desire to build twenty lines into Prince Albert or any other place, why should this House stand in the way? The*Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) in discussing the National Transcontinental-the government part of the line -and the government policy in relation to the building of roads, declared that it was a competitive policy, not a pioneer policy. Prom the standpoint of competition, it would be advisable for Prince Albert to have several roads. I quite approve of the stand taken by the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) that the amendment is irregular. In addition I do not think that it is in the interest of the people of the west that any charter held by a bona fide railway building company should be struck out.
Let the people of the west judge.
I ask the hon. member for Humboldt, or yourself, whether there has been a petition presented to this House against the renewal of this charter.

As far as notice of the intention of the company to apply for a renewal of the charter is concerns, frequently this notice is very limited, but I have had information that within a few days a very largely signed petition from the farmers all along the line would be forwarded to my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) and to myself protesting against a renewal of the charter unless the Canadian Pacific Railway guarantee to go on and build the road.
We had better wait until we see what they say.

In so far as this amendment not being in proper form to attain the result I desire is concerned, I have just to say that the clause referred to, in my motion, subsection A of section 9 of chapter 52 of the statutes of 1893, reads as follows:
An extension of the main line from the present terminus thereof at Yorkton, in a northwesterly direction to a point at or near Prince-Albert, on the north bank of the Saskatchewan river.
I am not going to say definitely-hon. gentlemen may say the opposite-that under Mr. J. A. CURRIE.
this charter the line has been extended to Sheho. That may be the case but I have this to say that in so far as using the charter for the purpose for which the charter is intended is concerned, it has not been used in that way from Yorkton to Prince Albert. No line has been built in the direction of Prince Albert from Yorkton. This line has already been extended westward showing what the original object of the Canadian Pacific Railway in so far as they _ have extended the line from Sheho practically to the town of Lanigan. It will be completed to Lanigan before the shipping season commences. The extension from Sheho is an extension in a westerly and not in a northwesterly direction. I do not care under what charter they built this particular line to Sheho; it does not affect the argument at all in favour of the amendment which seeks to cancel the charter that gives them power to build in a northwesterly direction to Prince Albert.

I do not like the members of this House to be misled by statements which must have that result. For instance, the first statement made is that this company do not intend to build this road. I do not know where hon. gentlemen get that information. I cannot get it. I assume that when they are asking for a renewal of this charter they do intend to build within two years.
What assurance can the hon. gentleman give?

The assurance that they are not asking for a renewal of this charter without a purpose. My hon. friend from Humboldt (Mr. Neely) states that the road has been built from Yorkton to Sheho in a westerly direction. That line runs in the direction of Prince Albert. Sheho is northwest _sf Yorkton. I forget the township although I ought to know because it is in my own constituency. The line runs in the direction of Prince Albert and the survey has been extended in as nearly a' direct line to Prince Albert as it would be possible to obtain. The hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) tries to make this committee believe that they have built to Sheho, but that this carries them west and that they are seeking authority to build their line from Lanigan. That is misleading. Lanigan is in another direction. It is on the Kirkella branch. When this railway got to Sheho it wanted to connect with the Kirkella branch so as to be on the main line to Edmonton. Therefore, they have built something like 50 miles of this line from Sheho to Lanigan.
82 miles.

They have built that distance to Wynward. They have graded the line to Sheho. To show that it is not their intention to run the main line to Lanigan I may state that they have graded the line part of the way to Fishing lake. They turn off af few miles from Sheho and then go west. I think there was some condition that they should build so much of each line each year. I imagine that their principal object in asking for this renewal at the present time is that they may complete the forty or fifty miles that they have already built of their western line towards Prince Albert. I see no reason why this renewal should not be granted. It seems to me that some hon. gentlemen have taken a great objection to the Canadian Pacific Railway because it is that particular line, not giving sufficient consideration to the fact that the people living in this neighbourhood are desirous of obtaining railway facilities. If they are desirous of obtaining railway facilities they can get this line quicker by having the Canadian Pacific Railway construct it than by having it constructed by a private company. It would take a private company a year to get their charter and we know that it is seldom that railway companies are able to go to work immediately after they get their charter. The result is that two years might elapse before actual operations are commenced.

We have heard considerable to-day about the influence of the railway and the influence of the people. I would just say that this appears to me very much like an effort on the part, not of the Canadian Pacific Railway, but of some other railway to keep the Canadian Pacific Railway out of Prince Albert. We found the same influence working against the wishes of the people in the construction of a branch line from Lanigan to Prince Albert. We know that it also has worked against the construction of other branch lines. We know that it is also the same influence which has been continuously working against the building of a line to Prince Albert on other occasions, but what we and the people wish to see in that western country is competition. That is what the people of the west, one and all, want. I would say that it is not 30, or 40 or 50 miles of this road that have been built but over 200 miles.
Mr. SPRt)ULE. 293 miles.
From Portage la Prairie I think it has been built?
Yes.

And what has been built is directly in line between York-ton and Prince Albert; so that, instead of using the line running by way of Fishing
lake and Lanigan, they have built a branch line from Fishing lake to Lanigan and in that way they have shown themselves entitled to more consideration and respect. They have finished nearly 82 miles of the branch lines from a little north of Sheho to Lanigan and while they have built a line to Lanigan they expect to build the other branch. They have pretty, nearly completed the branch line from Sheho to Lanigan, and they are now preparing to build the main line directly to Prince Albert. We must remember that Lanigan is 82 miles out of the way, and that the traffic of Prince Albert will be compelled to go 82 miles out of the way for all time if the construction of this line is prevented. Eighty-two miles in that country is a great distance and there is a large section of country adjacent to Lake Leonore that would be benefited by the construction of this branch line. During all the years I have been in this House I have never beard of a railway company that had built so many miles of railway or which had proceeded with the construction of its line in the same manner as this has been proceeded with and, having constructed 82 miles of a branch line covered by another and recently granted charter, and then having the charter for its partly constructed main line refused a renewal. It is perfectly absurd to say that they do not intend to proceed and complete the road, therefore the extension of their charter should certainly be granted, and the absurdity appears still stronger when I see the careless way in which the amendment has been drawn up, so careless indeed that even the'mover of the amendment has to admit that it does not say what he really meant it should say. I am surprised that a man living in the west, and living at Humboldt at that, should come here and know so little about his own country.

I would point out to hen. gentleman that the Railway Committee has laid down the principle this year, that they would not oppose the granting of such charters as this, and the Minister of Railways has himself emphatically stated two or three times in the House that such is the policy of parliament. I do not see how the members of the west are going to benefit their people by refusing to extend these charters. If I thought it would benefit the people I would vote in favour of it, because I have great sympathy with the people in the west who are badly in need of railway facilities in some districts. I have not the least doubt in the world that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company will build this line of railway and other lines similarly situated just as soon as they are able, and when this particular branch line is built it will be operated in connection with one of the largest and best managed railways in the world and

will afford every facility to the people, and I do not agree with the contention that the existence of this charter stops other people from getting charters, because I have not the slightest doubt that if any other company wants to build a railway over this route they can apply to parliament tomorrow and they will get a charter, probably	whether they	intend to	build	or not.This	is a prairie	country,	there	are nopasses to go through, there is room for any number of roads, and there is no blocking nr blanketing. I think the hon. gentlemen from	the Northwest who	have	spoken
against this Bill are standing in their own light.

I would point out to the hon. gentleman that this is not a prairie country, but on the contrary there are many hills	which the	railways	have	to go
through. I also want to tell hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House that there are many petitions from Prince Albert and from the people living in that section of the country opposing this charter. They have good reason to believe that the Canadian Pacific Kailway are not sincere in their intention to build. The people in that country believe that if this charter were out of the way they could deal with other people and get a line of railroad built quicker than the Canadian Pacific Railway would build it.
Does the hon. gentleman seriously believe that any company would build a little bit of a road like that ieading no where and commencing practically nowhere?	[DOT]

My experience both in the United States and in Canada 'is that many short lines of railroad have been built through new country, and although of course thev were afterwards devoured by the other companies, yet they afforded means of transportation to the settlers and relieved them from the disabilities under which they laboured. We cannot raise grain profitably and haul it 40 or 50 miles to a railroad; we must have railway transportation facilities or our land is of no value to us. I am entirely opposed to placing in the hands of the Canadian Pacific Railway, the Canadian Northern Railway, or the Grank Trunk Pacific either, the monopoly of building railways throughout that country, a monopoly which we practically give them if we allow them to blanket the country with charters, and come here year after year asking for extensions of time. It may be all right to have free trade in railway charters when you are granting new charters, but when you come to these renewals it is an entirely different thing. Now, I object to this system of the railway company including in one Bill legislation for the renewal of several charters. The Minister of Railways has Mr. NESBITT.
distinctly stated that we should deal with these charters each on its own merits, but so long as the railway companies jumble the whole thing up into one Bill for the purpose of misleading the people of the country it is impossible to treat each on its own merits. There are several branch lines included in this one Bill, and while it may be fair in the case of some of them to grant an extension of time, in other cases it undoubtedly should not be granted. We have the right to know now whether the Canadian Pacific Railway are ready to build this road or whether they simply intend to get an extension of time now and to come back a few years hence for a further extension. There has been settlement in that part of the province of Saskatchewan as long as in any other part of the province, and we have a right to expect that we. should have railway facilities. We know that it is the nolicy of the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian Northern Railway to divert settlement from one section of the country and to scatter it in other sections so that they may have the benefit of the long haul on the freight in and out, and that is no doubt a natural thing for a railway company to do in its own interest, but we certainly should not allow these railway companies to blanket the country with charters so as to prevent other roads from coming in there. Prince Albert needs another railway and Lake Leonore country wants a railway badly. People have been settled in there for five or six years; there is a large colony of French people who have settled there in the expectation that they were going to get a railway. They nave gone through a great deal of hardship, they have obtained accommodation until they were able to get their patents and they now want to relieve themselves of their obligations. Every gentleman in this House knows that if you have 169 acres of land twenty-five miles from a railway, even though it is the best land in the world, you cannot get a loan company to help you. I have been trying personally for the past few years to help some of these poor people. If I had the money myself I would be willing to lend it because I know the time will come when they will have a railway in there and then they will be able to meet their obligations, but you cannot get a loan company to take chances on that. There are people in some sections of that country who have been settled ten or fifteen years there and who are miles away from a railway and they would like now to experience some of the comforts of life. They do not want the road for their grandchildren, they wish to see it during their lives they would like to see the amendement; carry and this company who have shown no evidence of intention to build, should get out of the way and let

some other road have a chance to set in there.

I presume from the way the hon. gentleman has spoken that he does not desire either the Manitoba and Northwestern or the Canadian Pacific Railway to build this road at all.
42 miles of that line has been built and is already in operation. To cancel the charter would cancel their power of operation of these 42 miles and might get somebody into serious trouble. I do not think the House intends to do this, and I trust the committee will vote down the amendment.
It does not make one bit of difference to me who builds the road so long as we get it built.

Then why do you not approve of this charter?
. Mr. RUTAN. Because it has been in existence for 16 years under the Canadian Pacific Railway and we are no nearer getting it built that we were 16 years ago. I would say further that when this matter came before me and I had to investigate it to see if the Canadian Pacific Railway intended building into Prince Albert this year, I was plainly told by the man who knows that they were not going to build any of it this year, that their plans were all made. I asked whether they would build in another year and he said he could not say that, he might not be here and he did not want to say anything that would bind his successors.

I am not in the habit of interfering with any legislation affecting any part of the country which is better known to other hon. members than it is to myself. There is no doubt that the hon. members for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff), Prince Albert (Mr. Rutan) and Humboldt (Mr. Neely) have voiced the disappointment of their people, because they have been disappointed through not having the railway constructed before now; but I ask them if their arguments are of any weight to affect the judgment of this House? Have they any proof or guarantee that should the House not grant this extension of time, any company or individuals would build the road? Would it not be worse for their people if- we should torpid the Canadian Pacific Railway to build there? No private corporation will build in that country in opposition to the great companies now operating there, and I think it would be far better for these people if we should grant the extension and allow the Canadian Pacific Railway to build the road. The Canadian Pacific Railway has no interest in preventing the settlers from getting transportation.

speechtext:
I am sorry the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) is not in his seat this afternoon because the motion made by the hon member for Hum-bolt (Mr. Neely) deserves some answer from him. I know the views he entertains on that question and I can state them. All the considerations involved in the Bill and the amendment of my hon. friend have been, as I understand, discussed and considered by the Railway Committee, and while it is not an absolute rule it is a rule I think of great convenience and safety that when a matter of this kind has been considered by the Railway Committee the judgment of the the Railway Committee should be accepted, unless there be some very strong reason to the contrary. The only reason which has impressed me to-day is that advanced by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) that we should consult and abide by the wishes of the people in a matter of this kind. But what are the wishes of the people? There is a serious discrepancy as to that. Two of my friends on this side of the House state that the wishes of the people are against an extension of this charter, and on the other hand my hon. friend from Mackenzie (Mr. Cash) who is as much interested in this matter as any one else and who ought to know the country and the circumstances is strongly in favour of this extension. The argument made by my hon. friend

from Humboldt (Mr. Neely), supported by my hon. friend from Prince Albert (Mr. Rutan), is that the Canadian Pacific Railway have been remiss in the duty imposed on them by a charter as far back as 1883, and have not done anything. What is the reason? The reason is that to-day the western provinces are developing so rapidly that it is not possible to keep abreast of the demand for railways. At this moment if the Canadian Pacific Railway, the Canadian Northern and the Grand Trunk Pacific were to undertake the construction of 1,000 miles of railway each during the coming summer they would not meet all the requirements of the people of the country. The demand comes from all quarters for more railways, and if such a strong railway as the Canadian Pacific Railway has not been able up to the present time to meet the demands of the new settlers, is it to be supposed or believed that any other company could have done it? Suppose the Canadian Pacific Railway does not go on with this work? Is it to be supposed that an independent company will be formed and will be ready to undertake the task any sooner than the Canadian Pacific Railway will do it? 1 think not, and I think my hon. friends had better rely on the will of the Canadian Pacific Railway to perform this work. It is to their interest to do so. That section of the country is developing very Tapidly, as has been stated by the hon. member for Prince Albert, and therefore it is to the interest of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company to be able to serve that section of the country as soon as they can, and I think on the whole we had better rely on the judgment of the Railway Committee in this matter.
Amendment (Mr. Neely) negatived; Bill reported, read the third time and passed.
