The charter is unnecessary, apparently.

No, the whole question was fully discussed in the Railway Committee. I made the same statement there that I made here, that the road was being constructed. These people have taken the risk of going on with construction in advance of the charter. This is not the only road that has been gone on with in that way; I can assure my hon. friend (Mr. Boyce) that many railway companies have gone a little in advance of their charter where there was no possible difficulty to be met with. If there were highways to be considered, or surveys of municipalities, it would be different. This is what might be called a wilderness, except so far as the mining and lumbering to which I have referred are concerned.

We have been opposing these companies because they were not going on with the work, and not likely to do so. But this company seems to be going on. I remember that we had opposite?? to some clauses of this Bill in the "al]^ay Committee from a representative of the Ontario government. But, as the company is to go through and connect with the Grand Trunk Pacific it seems to me that is the reason why it should have a Dominion charter.
On section 9,

I understood from the promoter of the Bill, both here and in the Railway Committee, that this was a charter for a railway company. Apparently it is a charter'for a company very different-it is really a power company, and, under the provisions of this section, a most extraordinary power company.

I do not know whether this is the standard clause or not, nor do I care very much. This is a clause to permit the company to acquire power, and there is no limitation or restriction as

to the manner of acquiring that power, whether by generation or by taking over existing powers. There is no limitation to the localities in which it is to be acquired. It seems to me the committee^ is entitled to a very much fuller explanation of the objects of the company and its powers than is contained in the clause just read. In the first place, it is undoubtedly a power clause, and, in the opinion of many hon. members of this House, it is entirely within the control of the provincial legislature. The hon. gentleman who moves this Bill has more than once taken that stand in this House. I ask the hon. gentleman to explain what he means, what he proposes to do by the power clause, and what restriction he proposes to put upon the company with regard to generating that power, with regard to distance, and locality, and so on.

The clause is the usual clause that is inserted in nearly all the Railway Bills that are passed in' this House, there is no difference. It is a clause that is approved by the Railway Committee and by the Minister of Railways, and it has appeared I think in the majority of Bills. It is not giving to the company the general powers of a power company, it gives them power to expend their money as a corporate body for the purpose of acquiring water-power or generating electricity for the operation of their road; that is all.
There is power there to dispose of the surplus.
If they have more than they require for their own use, they may dispose of it. But that does hot constitute this company a power company instead of a Tailway company.
What would prevent it, as the Bill stands ?

What would prevent it in the other Bills ? This provision does not move this company out from under the general law of the province or of the Dominion. How are they going to become a power company ? They are subject to all the restrictions and conditions of the provincial law. They have got to acquire the water-power; this Bill does not empower them to take water from any particular place.
It allows them to do it everywhere.
Not at all, only for the operation of their road. At the present time power is merely an incidental.
They have no power of expropriation.

They have got to show that they want it for their Toad, that is Mr. MACDONELL.
the first thing. But incidentally if they have more than they want, who wishes to prevent them from selling it ?

It is not in the Bill, but I want to ask the hon. member why should it be in the Bill? Is it in any other Bill? There is no power under this Bill to expropriate a water-power, they have the power of the Railway Act for the pnrpose of constructing their railway only. This clause has been adopted in other Bills, why object to it in this case? If there is any Bill I know of that has passed this House in recent yeaTS where such a power ought to be given, it should be given to a road of this character that is being built in an absolutely new country, entirely unsettled, and unoccupied except by mines, lumbering and construction.
Suppose that a waterpower had been developed so as to generate electricity and they acquired control oyer it, would they not then have control over it?

If a company owned a water-power and developed it, and obtained it from either the Dominion or provincial authority, that company would be bound by the conditions under which they obtained the power to develop it, and if this company acquired it they would be bound by the same conditions. I know of nothing that would prevent a company from selling a water-power. But that is not the point in this Bill, the point is, does this give power to expropriate and take it without consent of the owner ?
Does this railway cross the Nipigon river ?
No, it is about 200 miles west of the Nipigon river.
What river does it cross ?

I do not think it crosses any river, it runs along what is called the English river for a portion of the way which, is I believe in some sections of its course an interprovincial boundary between the province and the district of Kee-watin.

I think the hon. gentleman is promoting his Bill very cleverly, but I cannot adopt his view that because the Bill is silent as to the right to expropriate that therefore they could not expropriate. Why, they could not expropriate for railway purposes according to his argument. The Bill itself does not give him the right to expropriate. They can go on and construct and operate a railway, but not a

word about expropriation. The hon. gentleman will not admit that he cannot expropriate for railway purposes under the Railway Act. And they go on and say that for the purpose of the undertaking they may also acquire these water-powers.

This company has not got specific powers of expropriation in the Bill, but they have them under the Railway Act. Then they are thrown back on the Railway Act, and how could my hon. friend argue that the Railway Act gave this company power to expropriate a water-power ?

I did not say they could, but I say it could be well argued before a court that inasmuch as the special Act gave them the right to acquire these water-powers and that the Railway Act applies to it, they would have the same right-whether by expropriation or by private purchase, in regard to the one matter as to the other. If they are going to take water-powers by expropriation when people are not willing to sell them, they will be causing a great deal of trouble. Even if it was limited to the purposes of the undertaking, I think the point is just the same. 'Fot the purpose of the undertaking' means for the purpose of carrying on everything that is authorized by this charter. Then without the words of limitation that you cannot expropriate, certainly when you say you want the water-power for the purpose of using and working the railway, you can at once use every right of expropriation that you could for the other purposes of the undertaking.

I cannot think upon reflection that my hon. friend (Mr. Lancaster) will adhere to the view which he has just expressed. There is no power contained in this Bill to expropriate land. As far as the railway is concerned, the Railway Act would apply. Then, we have to look to the Railway Act to see what are the powers of expropriation which are there given and they are to expropriate a right for the railway of, I think, not exceeding six rods in width and what is necessary for station purposes. That is the only land which can be expropriated under the Railway Act.

That is to say that they do not have this power but practically we declare in this charter that they may do these other things for the purpose of this undertaking. The special Act extends the Railway Act and makes it apply to the very things in question.
If this Act contained a clause saying that the provision of the Railway Act should apply to all properties that the company might* desire to acquire for the purposes of the undertaking.
Is not that so ?

No, it is not, because all this Act does is to give to the company the power to acquire land; that is to acquire it in the ordinary legal way by agreement with the people who- happen to own it. The company is not given power to take land without the consent of the party who owns it. The only power of expropriation which exists is the power which is contained in the Railway Act and that is limited to six rods in width for the right of way and such lands as may be necessary for station purposes. If a water-power happened to be within the right of way or within the six rods, of course, it might be acquired by expropriation.

That is exactly where the acuteness of the company would cause them to operate. If they should say: We will put this line of railway within the 90 or 100 feet belt that we are allowed to-expropriate and thereby take in a water-power, under the Bill they could do it.
They might do that.
Exactly; and yet it stated distinctly that they are not going to expropriate water-powers.

I would like to ask the -hon. gentleman who has charge of this Bill why they want water-powers to operate this railwav. When the Bill was before the Railway Committee the understanding was that this was to be a railway operated by steam entirely. Now we all know that if there are any water-powers in the district between the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Grand Trunk Pacific they are all entirely within the control of the Ontario government, and if this clause is allowed to remain in, such a thing might occur as my hon. friend from Lincoln (Mr. I.ancaster) has just stated. They might run this railway 20 or 30 miles along one of these rivers, expropriate a water-power and the Ontario government could not interfere. If that is the object of the Bill we certainly must have a different impression of it than that which was sought to be conveyed in the Railway Committee. When it was stated that the usual standard clause as far as water-powers are concerned was to be put into the Bill nobody ever thought it meant what has been suggested here today. I was in favour of the Bill and am nowr in favour of the granting of a charter by this parliament provided it does not mean practically taking all the water-powers in that district and locking them up. I do not see why the clause referring to water-powers should not be dropped. We were assured in the Railway Committee that this was a railway to be constructed from



the Canadian Pacific Railway to the Grand Trunk Pacific and that it was to be a steam railway throughout its whole length. With reference to the clause dealing with boats and docks, it was mentioned by the hon. gentleman in charge of the Bill that-they might want to run boats on the lakes and take people to summer resorts. There was no objection to that. But it seems to me, from the discussion which has taken place, that there is another object altogether behind this Bill. I think it would be better to refer the Bill back to the Railway Committee and let us get it thoroughly threshed out there rather than to try to push it through here to-day in its present form and containing a clause the effect of which we may not be able at the present time to fully appreciate.
This is the same clause that we have put in practically every railway charter.
No.

Most of them. This clause has appeared in most of the charters that have passed through the Railway Committee during the present and previous sessions. The fact that this is a steam railway should not prevent the company at some future time, if it found it advisable to run their trains by electricity, from adopting that motive power. The Canadian Pacific Railway is a steam railway and at the present time the management have under consideration the electrifying of certain portions of the line. I do not think my hon. friends need be alarmed about the power of expropriation where it only extends to a strip of land six rods wide. Any one knows that they could not have a waterpower and a railway working together on a right of way of that width.
How would it be crossing the Tiver.

It might be possible, but I do not think it would be. Railways do not want a water-power right at a bridge where they cross, because there is always the danger of the dam going out and taking away the railway bridge. The clause is one which we have put in before, and I do not see any reason why this particular Bill should be picked out or why the same provisions should not be given to this company as are given to others.

Will the hon. gentleman name any charter that has passed this House within the last two or three years containing a clause such as this? I do not know of any, and I am a pretty regular attendant at the Railway Committee. I never saw such a clause as that in a Steam Railway Bill in my life.

When this Bill was before the Railway Committee the clause dealing with water-powers was withdrawn and the model clause which the Railway Committee have accepted with regard to water-powers was inserted in lieu of it. This is the model clause.
What does the hon. gentleman mean by the model clause? I am afraid he is dignifying this with a name that it is not entitled to.

That is what it was called by the chairman and it was inserted. My hon. friend is borrowing trouble when he imagines that the railway company might run its line purposely to get a water-power. I wonder if the Railway Board or the Minister of Railways would ratify the plans of a railway company that would try a trick like that?

They might not know it.
M" CONMEE. They would know it. It would be plain because it would require 60 or 100 acres to enable any person to operate a water-power. It would be absolutely useless in the charter. It is only borrowing trouble; it is a suspicion without any foundation.

I am afraid I am not borrowing trouble. I wish I were because I do not want to keep this discussion up unnecessarily. This clause says that this power shall be exercised subject to section 247 of the Railway Act. That strengthens my argument and strengthens the contention o.f my hon. friend from Grenville (Mr. Reid). The Railway Act is brought in and then this special Act is brought in and it provides that this power can be exercised provided it does not interfere with section 247 of the Railway Act. It may be held that as long as it does not conflict with section 247 of the Railway Act the provi sions of the Railway Act are complied with.
Section 247 presupposes that these rights will be purchased, and it simply restricts them from using them on the highways without the consent of the municipalities. Then, if the municipalities cannot agree with the company, the Railway Board decides upon what conditions these rights are to be acquired. How can my hon. friend contend that it is quite sure they cannot expropriate. My point is that this charter is made subject to section 247 only, and 247 provides that you must not put your lines and poles along the highway without the consent of the municipality, and if the municipality does not consent you have to go to the board, who can order in what manner the wires shall be placed.

By section 3 of the Act passed last year respecting the Edmonton Dunvegan and British Columbia Railway

even broader power is given than is contained in this Bill.
But that Act does not say that the company is subject to section 247 of the Railway Act. It does seem to me that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Con-mee) is in this Bill getting much more than he wants.
Oh no, he could not.

The hon. gentleman tells us that he does not want expropriation powers and I have to accept his word. If the hon. gentleman does not want power to expropriate it is very easy to insert words excluding that power.
In the Edmonton, Yukon and Pacific Railway Act, also passed last year, there are still broader powers given to acquire for the purpose of developing electricity.
All that shows that this is not a model Bill.
It might be called a *modest Bill.

In Bill (No. 11) passed this session respecting the Canadian Western Railway Company, there is a clause subjecting it to the provisions of 247 of the Railway Act, as to the charges which may be made for electricity, &c., and the Board of Railway Commissioners have the power to decide.
Did that Bill pass as the hon. gentleman has read it?
I think there was no change whatever made in that Bill.

Why is it that the Bill referred to by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Turriff) subjects that company to the provisions of section 247 of the Railway Act, while the Bill mentioned by the Minister of Public Works does not?
The Bills I refer to were passed last session.
It is because of amendments to the Railway Act which gives the board powers they did not have before. It is a further protection for the public; that is all.

It is all right to say it is a further protection to the public, but when you make this company subject to one specific clause of the Railway Act, any court will decide that you have not restricted it in any other way than in re spect to whatever restrictions may be in that particular clause. Under section 247 the board may order that the wires shall be placed in a certain way for the protection of the people, and that being so you cannot work out section 247 unless you do give them power to expropriate under eer-125i
tain conditions to be decided by the board. If this House is of opinion they should have power to expropriate that is one thing, but if we are deciding they should not' have power to expropriate then the Bill should say so.

At one time the law was that unless a company were restricted down to certain things they could do anything which they were not prevented specifically from doing in their charter. If it were fairly within the bounds of their charter the courts held they could do that thing whatever it was, if it could be said to be akin to their business. But that is not the law to-day and that has not been the law for the past ten years. The law i3 now that before a company can do any specific thing it must be set forth in its charter.
It says so in this charter.
There is nothing in this charter so far as I can see that specifically gives this company the right to expropriate.

It says they may acquire.
Mr McKENZIE That is not expropriation. I should judge from the manner in which my hon friend (Mr Lancaster) discusses questions in this House that he is a good lawyer and he knows that there is nothing by inference to be decided in favour of a corporation. There is no intendment in their favour at all. The power must be defined in clear language, and particularly a power so drastic as expropriation. They cannot by inference, or by reading half a dozen Acts together patch up a case for expropriation. The power must be given specifically, and if it is not given specifically the court will decide it was not intended they should have it.

It is not a matter of inference, it Ks a matter of the gentleman opposing the Bill thinking there is a limitation that is not expressed in the Bill that the railway company 'may acqu'ire.' I contend that there is no limit in the way of acquiring, it is not a matter of inference but a direct statement that ^ they can acquire whatever any other railway company can acquire.

That is what I said. The Railway Act is construed by the courts in the light of its purpose and will not be strained by them to give any corporation the right to get water-power which, as a rule, is not used ,in connection with railways. From my knowledge of corporation law and the common law generally I do not think there is need to be alarmed. This provision has been inserted lin several other Bills. I do not think an argument in

favour of expropriation of water-power could be based under this Bill.

The point I desire to make is with regard to the power th'is company is seeking to acquire in connection with the generation and sale of electricity. I asked the promoter to explain that and he explained it partly. I am not opposing the Bill as a railway Bill, I desire to he perfectly fair, but I am opposing it inasmuch as it is a power Bill. The promoter says that the Bill as it stands now would make the company subject to the general legislation of the province of Ontario regarding electric companies generating and selling and dealing in electric power and fluid. I differ from the hon. member principally because of section 2, which declares th'is work to be one for the general advantage of Canada which, as my hon. friend knows, brings it by the force of the British North America Act directly under the control and legislation of the Dominion parliament, so that it would pass av/ay from the control and jurisdiction of the provincial parliament. That is to my mind the effect of this Bill, it will be freed entirely from the effect of the general legislation of the province of Ontario regarding electric companies. It would also be freed from the general legislation of the province regarding railway companies, because the undertaking is declared to be for the general advantage of Canada. It thereupon ceases to be a provincial undertaking. My hon. friend says that as the Bill is worded the company would still be under provincial control. If he will submit to an amendment simply declaring that it is subject to the general legislation of Ontario regarding electric power companies, the Bill might pass. Several other Bills have that clause.
What Bill has that clause in?
A number of railway Bills. The charter for running the railway in this city has that clause. Such an amendment would remove the objection of my hon. friend from Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster).
That is an electric railway.
Because the general legislation of Ontario regarding electric companies provides safeguards regarding expropriation for electric purposes.
My statement was that this company would be subject to any general law of the province or of the Dominion affecting its works.

What objection is there to putting in a clause to that effect?
Mr. McKenzie.

There is a great deal of objection to putting in a clause to that effect. There is this objecion that it is unfair to put burdens upon this company and surround it with legislation different from that applying to other companies.
Why?

Simply because this company are here within their rights asking for certain _ legislation. If it is the general rule of this parliament to give general powers, why insert such a restriction in this Bill?
The hon. member says there is no power of expropriation; then why not specify it?

*You might say why do you not do many things. The general law of this province will apply to this company, and its acts just as to any other company. The declaration that it is for the general advantage of Canada will only affect it so far as it is a railway. The moment the company go outside of their railway work and establish workshops, the general Factory Act of the province, for instance, will apply.
Oh, no; oh, no.
Oh. yes; oh, yes.
By declaring it to be for the general advantage of Canada you remove it from provincial control.
Not at all.
Does the hon. gentleman think that by statute from this government he can get water-power?

Certainly, I think this is the only government that can grant powers in certain cases. I do not know anything about the water-power that this company have in view, I do not know if there is any. The Act to incorporate the Vancouver Island and Eastern Railway Company passed last session containing exactly the same clause, word for word.

The hon. gentleman states that there will be no expropriation powers as far as water-powers and electric development are concerned, that that will apply only to the railway. I would suggest as a solution of the difficulty that the word ' Tailway ' be inserted in clause 2 so that it will read:
The railway undertaking of the company is declared to be a work for the general advantages of Canada.
That will settle all the trouble and the Bill could go through.

That may be a very reasonable proposition, but I am only the member to whom this Bill has been referred and I would not undertake to make any changes

in it; it is for the promoters to advise me through their solicitors and so far as I am concerned I would not agree to any amendment.

It is not quite for the promoters and their solicitor to say what legislation we shall pass. We are here to pass legislation in the interests of the people. I think the suggestion of the hon. member for South Toronto (Mr. Macdonell) is most reasonable; it would carry out what we all intend. But I want to settle with the hon. member for Rainy River (Mr. Conmee) this question. I want to understand whether he means that the whole of the undertaking will not be for the general advantage of Canada if this Bill passes. Does he really believe that the water-powers will be in any different position from the railway when the whole Bill is declared for the general advantage of Canada.

There is no power under this Bill by which this company could expropriate a water-power. As to the question whether its particular works, after they are established, in so far as they relate to its actual undertaking, might be somewhat removed from provincial legislation or not, I am not prepared to say because I do not profess to have any information on that point.

What harm will be done by putting in a clause, such as suggested by the hon. member for South Toronto, to the effect that the provincial laws shall apply to the regulation and expropriation of these water-powers ?
I would not agree to that.
Then the hon. gentleman means to override provincial legislation ?

No, but I would not agree because that would prohibit the company taking a water-power which would be on an international or a navigable stream. I do not propose to have the hands of the company tied up by any such a condition.

We must not tie our own hands by giving to the company what they should not have. Between now and eight o'clock the hon. gentleman had better consider that.
At six o'clock, committee took recess.
After Recess.
Committee resumed at eight o'clock.

Before we rose at six o'clock, I asked the promoter of the Bill what reason he had to give for incorporating in a railway Bill power privileges, and especially when as under section 2, all the works of the company are declared to be works for the general advantage of Canada. I can quite understand why this provision bringing the company's works under the control of this parliament should be passed in relation to a railway company of this kind. But here is a purely provincial adjunct inserted in this Bill, here is a clause dealing with a purely provincial matter, and yet this part of the works of the company is also brought under the control of this parliament and removed from the control of the province. The promoter of the Bill, if I understood him aright, said that the sections to which I refer had not the effect I attribute to it. But I refer the hon. gentleman to the well known section 92 of the British North America Act, subsection 10, clause (c). As we all know, section 92 deals with those powers which are exclusively within the control of the provincial legislature. Subsection 10 declares that local works and undertakings other than certain classes enumerated are provincial undertakings. Of these exceptions clause (c) relates to ' such works as, though wholly situate within the province are before, or after execution declared by the parliament of Canada to be for the general advantage of Canada or for the advantage of two or more of the provinces.' By this declaration under the authority of this clause, these works and undertakings of this company are removed from provincial jurisdiction. As the promoter (Mr. Conmee) before recess gave it as his opinion that the works of the company, so far as they related to power distribution are provincial in their character, I think it only fair that he should insert in this Bill a declaration that, so far as these works are concerned, they are excepted from the declaration as to the works of this company being for the general advantage of Canada. Or, as an alternative, let the hon. gentleman make it plain that the law of Ontario relating to electric companies, including the Hydro-Electric Power Commission Act, shall apply to this part of the company's undertakings. Then the hon. gentleman will have the powers he wants, and the others will remain subject to the jurisdiction of the province. Whoever heard of the undertakings of a power company, wholly within one province and purely local in their character, being declared works for the general advantage of Canada? It was stated this afternoon that this power clause is what is called the model power clause. I never heard of a model power clause in any railway company's Bill. I can understand a model power clause in a power Bill. But this is primarily a railway Bill, and I am not aware of any practice in regard to this model clause in the case of such Bills. There is none, so far as this House is aware, and if there is a model clause, it surely does not apply to merely provincial undertakings. I think the promoter should give some better reason than he has given

why these works, purely provincial in their nature, should be declared works for the general advantage of Canada. There is no desire to obstruct this Bill. As a railway company's charter, I quite agree with it. I think this undertaking is a Dominion undertaking, as it connects with the Transatlantic line. But, as a power company Bill, I object to it being brought under Dominion control.

I find, on looking over the Bills that have been before the House this session, that the clause giving these same powers have been embodied in Bills Nos. 11, 44, 50, 59 and 62. It is also in Bill 102, which has passed the Railway Committee, but has not yet passed this Committee of the Whole. But these powers have been granted in the Railway Committee, and supported by all those gentlemen who are now opposing this Bill. In all these Bills, the only change that was made was to substitute the model clause for the clause that happened to be in the Bill. I do not know that this power has been refused to any railway company that has asked for it, and I fail to see why this railway company should be selected for refusal of these powers especially when the matter i3 placed under control of the Railway Commission as it is in this Bill.

I have not had time to look up the Bills to which the hon. gentleman refers, but in the first one I look at, which is the last one he mentioned, No. 102, I find-and I suppose, should find it in all the others-the same words that I am now contending for.

That clause wa3 taken out of the Bill in the Railway Committee, for the reason that the minister rather objected to that character of legislation, and in lieu of it was substituted the very same clause that is in this Bill.

So far as I understand the clause, it does not seem to be very objectionable, but I think it is liable to the very abuses which my hon. friend from Lincoln referred to before six o'clock. Moreover, the hon. gentleman promoting the Bill has a reputation that is so well known, both in this parliament and in another, that though his name is not placarded on the outside of the Bill, we suspect this hon. gentleman's sign manual is to be found somewhere in it. That is what makes every one suspicious of the Bill, and therefore we are obliged to look into it more carefully than we would other Bills.
Order.

I am merely saying that the sign manual, the astute Chinese nand, i3 to be found somewhere in the Bill. We are consequently doubly suspicious of any Bill which that hon. gentleman introduces Mr. MACDONELL
here, because we fear that there is something occult in it, something that is not disclosed at the first reading. In other respects I do not see anything very objectionable in it.
I suppose the hon. gentleman feels that the Bill introduced by the member for London (Mr. Beattie), which is in identical words, is all right?

I was not referring to that at all. I have not read the Bill introduced by the hon. member for London, and the hon. Minister of Public Works is a little too previous, as he usually is. He is attributing to me something that emanates from, I was going to say the evil designs of an evil heart. ' Evil be to him who evil thinks.' So far as this Bill gives the right to construct a railway, and operate a railway and railway property, I am sure that, so far as I can judge the sense of this side of the House, there is no objection to it whatever. But it is because we believe that it is intended to carry the right to take over, or expropriate, or secure control of water-powers that are to-day under the control of the provincial government, and upon which they have announced their policy to the world as one which they desire to carry out in the future-it is because of that danger that we look upon this Bill with suspicion. The hon. member himself says that it is subject to the control of the provincial government, which every parliamentarian knows it cannot be and could not be, by any provision which is in the Bill to-day. I think the hon. member went further and stated that he had the consent of the Ontario government, and their approbation of this Bill. But how can he reconcile that statement with the fact that the Ontario government has sent one of their supporters down here to oppose the Bill. If they were satisfied with it and had given their approval, why should they send a man here to oppose it? That is what increases our suspicion. I think therefore we should try and make this enactment as plain as possible, so that no abuses may develop afterwards.
The hon. member I fhink has told the truth in one respect. Because he happens to see in the Bill the namq of the member who is promoting it, he is suspicious of it.
That goes a long way, I confess.

They say that open confession is good for the soul, so I suppose my hon. friend is relieved now that he has got that off. Then he says that those who know the hon. member are suspicious of the Bill. Now, he is wrong in that. It is because my hon. friend does not know the hon. member who is promoting the Bill that he is suspicious. I guarantee that he

cannot find any one who does know him, whether he be Liberal or Conservative, who will give him the character that the hon. gentleman would like to impute to him.
My hon. friend behind me (Mr. Macdonell) sees it in the same way.

Perhaps he is as prejudiced as the hon. member for Grey (Mr. Sproule), and objects to the Bill for the same reason. Now, I did not say that the Ontario government approved of this Bill; what I said was that I was apprised that the Ontario government were giving them the right of way free.
Did not the hon. gentleman say the Ontario government had approved of this Bill?

No, I did not. As a matter of fact, I think they have approved of it. But what I stated was that they had given it a land bonus, although it was not yet actually chartered, and they did so knowing that the application for a charter was made to this parliament and not to the legislature. They I assume are not prejudiced agaipst this Bill.
Why did they send their representative here to oppose it?

I do not know, but I will give the hon. member my opinion. I think that the legal gentleman who appeared here was not instructed to oppose this Bill particularly. He is here as the representative of Ontario to oppose all Bills that, in his judgment, he thinks conflicts with provincial rights, and he opposed this Bill as he opposed a dozen other Bills, and for no other reason. It is not conceivable that the Ontario government would grant a bonus to a company if they had serious objection to their charter, and they knew the company was getting their charter here.
When did they grant the bonus, and what did the bonus consist of?
Land. The hon. member will see it reported in the returns and in the press. For this very railway they gave 1,000 acres of land per mile, as I understand the return.
The Superior and Western?
Yes.
Could the hon. gentleman say the distance this line is projected?
About 125 miles from the branch to the main line.
Can he give the House any information about the waterways that lie on the route of the railway?

So far as I have personal knowledge there are no water-powers. I believe they go close to what is known as the English river. It is merely a branch of the Albany river, but whether there are water-powers on the line I do not know. They go to Sturgeon lake and I think in passing north they pass what is known as the English river. I am not sure whether it is the English river or the Albany river which is right close to it at that point which forms the boundary between Ontario and Keewatin, but one or the other does.
Do I understand the hon. gentleman to say that this road has already been surveyed and that the work is under construction? If so, how much has been surveyed and constructed?
I am not aware of how much has been surveyed but the road has been located to Sturgeon lake and my information is that a portion is under construction. They are grading now.
How much is under construction?
About seven miles.

Does the hon. gentleman consider that this Bill considers power company clauses? If so, does he consider that this is the proper authority to grant a charter to a power company whose works are entirely within the bord-ersl of a province and in no way touch or affect international or interprovincial waters?

In regard to this being the proper authority to give the powers, that would depend. If the waters affected were interprovincial, or international, or
navigable
I excepted that.
This would be the proper authority. If it were otherwise I would assume that perhaps the legislature would have the control.
Are the waters with which this Bill is concerned interprovincial, international or navigable?
I am not prepared to say that they are interprovincial but I do say that they are navigable as far as I know.

I think this matter is of sufficient importance for the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) to give the committee an opinion upon it. I do not wish to be a party to any Bill that would interfere with provincial rights over water-powers. I do not think the Minister

of Railways would consent to the adoption of any such policy by this parliament. I am quite sure that he is conversant with this question and that he will give us his opinion upon the subject.

This Bill was thoroughly discussed in the committee and all these points were raised. They were ^ raised also, in so far as the Bills are identical, against the Bill introduced by the hon. member for London (Mr. Beattie). The clause to which the hon. member for South Toronto (Mr. Macdonell) refers as to water-powers, he will find, I think, in the great majority of the railway Bills by which charters have been given in recent years. There was a clause in the Bill introduced by the hon. member for London, such as the hon. member for South Toronto suggests, but the committee, without any dissenting voice, struck it out and put into the Bills the usual clause that we have put into other railway Bills governing the question of the right to distribute surplus power.
The same clause as this?

The clause we put into the other Bill is the clause we put into this. My hon. friend will remember that we struck out certain clauses and left the clerk to put in what we call' the model clause because that clause was one which was decided upon by the committee, not this session, but on a previous occasion as one which should be introduced into Bills of this character. As to this being for the general advantage of Canada, I do not think it is an extreme view to say that in so far as practicable every railway that does a general business should have a charter granted by this House so as to place it under the control of the Railway Commission and thus secure uniform rates. As to the power of expropriation, this Bill does not give the company any extraordinary rightsvwith regard to water-powers.

They would have to buy them. They cannot expropriate water powers under this Act.

TERMINAL AND TRANSFER ELEVATORS-GOVERNMENT OPERATION. Mr. F. L. SCHAFFNER (Souris). I beg to move the following resolution which stands in my name:

That in the opinion of this House the present system of operating terminal and transfer elevators is detrimental to the interests of the western gram producers, and that the government should itake immediate steps to operate terminal elevators at Fort William and Port Arthur, and the transfer elevators between those terminals and the Atlantic seaboard
I cannot help saying at once that I feel my inability to present the subject covered by this motion in the manner in which it should be presented; at the same time, I cannot help saying also that I feel honoured in having the opportunity to move a resolution so important as this. Having spent a little time in the study of the subject, I am thoroughly convinced that the grain elevator question is one of the most important to come before this parliament and I am equally convinced that, in a few years, the country will so regard it. We have been all day. talking on transportation questions. I do not say that we have spent too much time. Everybody admits, who has been in this parliament a few years, that the transportation question of necessity and rightly occupies a great deal of the time of the House. This question of grain elevators is so closely allied with the question of transportation that we cannot separate the two, and, when we take up so much time in discussing transportation, our time cannot but be well spent when we discuss the pros and cons-if there are any cons-of this resolution dealing with this vitally important question. Sometimes we are criticised because our resolutions are local or sectional. I do not think that criticism applies to the resolution which I now place before you Mr. Speaker. This resolution affects Canada from the Pacific to the Atlantic, and I for one hope that soon it will affect Canada from Hudson bay to our southern boundary. Let me say at once that I have no desire to make this a party question; I believe it is too big and too far-reaching to be considered in that light. I am confident that, at least so far as the members of the House from the western provinces are concerned, I shall have their sympathetic support regardless of their party affiliations.
This question of grain elevators is one which has agitated the minds of western people for a very long time. I find, in talking the matter over with eastern men, with the men of our financial centres if you like, that they have heretofore failed to grasp the importance of this question of our grain elevators as it affects the producers, and not only as it affects the producers, but also as it affects our financial centres as well.
You will observe that my resolution is confined, so far as its words are concerned, '
to terminal and transfer elevators. But the internal elevators are so closely allied to terminal and transfer elevators, that I hope you, Mr. Speaker, and this House, will not consider me out of order if I incidentally refer to this class that are not specifically mentioned in the resolution. I find-not on the part of western members, but of eastern members,-the lack of a clear definition in their minds of the three sets of elevators to which I have referred. Without occupying unnecessary time, let me give a definition of these three classes. We have, first, our internal grain elevators, scattered all over the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba. Wherever there is a railway, even a branch railway, the first thing that appears in some places and sometimes the only thing that appears,-I was going to say in a town, but I will say in a settlement is a grain elevator. Before I get through I intend to show though briefly how many of these elevators existed up to 1908. If our point of observation could be high enough, and our range of vision long enough, we could see a very large number of elevators scattered all over the western provinces. These elevators are the buildings in which the farmer deposits his grain from the wagon in which he has hauled it. There are loading platforms, of course, and according to the Act farmers are permitted to load their grain on to cars direct. But, as a rule-and I personally believe it is a legitimate and proper way and most convenient way to handle grain- the grain is put through the 'elevator. The veins of circulation by which this grain is brought to Winnipeg are numerous. After it reaches Winnipeg, there are two great arteries to carry it to the head of the lake. We hope soon to have three. We have the Canadian Pacific Railway, and the Canadian Northern, and I hope from the bottom of my heart-and it cannot be too soon,-we shall have the Grand Trunk Pacific. This will give us three great arteries emptying the grain( from these three provinces into what is called the terminal ele-votors at Port Arthur and Fort William. We have also what are called transfer elevators. After this grain reaches Port Arthur and Fort William and is placed in the terminal elevators, it is either carried by boat to Kingston, Montreal, Goderich or some other port, or it is taken all-rail to St. John. The transfer elevators are the links between the terminal elevators at Port Arthur and Fort William and the Atlantic coast where the grain is shipped to go to the markets of the world. The House can easily see what a complete chain there is in these elevators. And, so far as the producer is concerned, it is absolutely im-

399(5
possible to separate these elevators in our argument.
I do not stand here to say that government ownership is to be the great panacea for all alleged grievances in the state today. But I do say that according to the great law of selection, there are industries to which government ownership is applicable, and I believe there is no industry more so than this one of terminal elevators.
I do not minimize for a moment the tremendous difficulties that surround this question, I admit at once there are difficulties that will have to be overcome in connection with the government ownership of these terminal and transfer elevators, but I believe that when this government makes an honest and earnest effort to meet those difficulties, they will find them to be far less formidable than they appear. As to this question of terminal elevators, I am sure that every western man who has been in that country for some time will agree with me that it is a source of great agitation. Having spent about twenty-five years of my active life in the west, and having spent some years before that in the far east, I think I can realize perhaps better than some others how closely the west is connected with the east. I realize tonight, and I have realized many times in this House, how these two sections of our country are mutually dependent on each other. Within the last few days I have heard the remark: Why aTe these men talking all the time about the west? Why, there would not be any west if there were no east. That is quite true. I say that western Canada and eastern Canada are to-day component parts, and interdependent. You have your great financial centres, you have your manufacturing institutions that are absolutely necessary for us in the west. Only the other day an hon. gentleman on the other side of the House, a gentleman whom I very much respect, a gentleman who is engaged in a very large industry, came to me and said: Have you people in the west yet determined the amount of grain that you produced last year?* He said, You have made estimates during the summer, but what I would like to know as a manufacturer is whether you people have as yet realized to its full extent the amount of grain your country will produce?' He said, 'I do not believe you of the west understand how we people in the east are dependent upon your crops. When you have a good crop I can sell my machinery, and I can get my pay for it.' Well, I think that bears out a sentiment which I wish to express, that it is not a question of the west against the east. farmers up to a few years ago had not recognized this great principle of concerted action, they failed to apply the great principle of co-operation in order to get the best results, either for capital or for labour. Had the farmers co-operated, as they might have done, and as other industries in Canada have co-operated, they would not now be in the position in which they find themselves. Let me give one or two examples. Take the manufacturers. Have they been going for the last dozen or twenty years on their own hook, as the individual farmer apparently has been. The manufacturers in each line of business have associations among themselves, but there is one great association comprising them all, called the Manufacturers' Association. What do they do? "What are some of the problems these manufacturers have solved? They have their freight rates, they have their competition. they have the tariff, and many another problem coming before them for solution. But they have adopted concerted action, they co-operate, and are thereby able to meet these problems more successfully. When the Finance Minister of this country talks about changing the tariff, we find the manufacturers getting together, coming down here with delegation after delegation to visit the Minister of Finance and members of the government, and placing before them their propositions they go further. They know that^ people are human, and I have not the slightest doubt in the world that the ministers of this government are just as human as anybody else. What is the first thing they do? What do we find around the*e corridors almost every day of the session? A private member has a railway he wants built or a company has a railway it wants built. You find them, not coming as they formerly did on their own hook, and trusting to providence that their railway scheme will go through as they desire to have it, but they employ the very best lawyers in this country to come and plead for their

undertaking-all of which is perfectly legitimate.
Now apply that method of action to the farmers. I say that the farmers, for some reason or other, have been slow to recognize this principle of co-operation. But I assure you there is not a gentleman here from the west to-night but will hear me out in saying that the farmer is waking up, he is beginning to realize his needs and his power. I would advise this government, as I did the other day, and I would advise the leader of the opposition, that if they want to be in the running they had better pay more attention to what the farmers say and what the farmers are doing than they appear to do at present. In my own constituency of Souris I will guarantee that there are.twenty associations of grain growers. What is true of my constituency I am sure is true of every western constituency. These men seem to he very much in earnest, and all they have to do to get their rights is to go about it in earnest, and tell the government that if they want to get their votes they must give them what they want. The twenty associations in the constituency meet together. They elect delegates to the provincial association. Saskatchewan does the same thing. The association there is under the same name, while in Alberta, although it is practically the same organization, it is called, I think, the farmer's association. But, they are not content with that. They have what they call an interprovincial association which is made up of delegates from the different associations. The one question that has received the most careful consideration of this association during the past three years is the elevator question, not only as affecting internal, but also as affecting terminal and transfer elevators. As far as internal elevators are concerned the question was considered so important by the farmers of Manitoba, Alberta and Saskatchewan that they called upon the premiers to meet them in conference and discuss it. This meeting is rendered still more interesting by the fact that these premiers are not all upon the same side of politics, there being a Conservative government in the province of Manitoba and Liberal governments in the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta. I do not think these premiers, Grit or Tory, were particularly anxious to meet upon this question, but they did. They met because they have begun to feel in that western country that the farmer has to be listened to. They met delegates from the farmers' association. They sat for some time and then, like the wise judge who is not sure of what he is going to do, they reserved judgment. They did not give the farmers an answer at that time. It was not very long, however, before these three premiers gave judgment, and it was adverse to the taking over of the internal elevators. But that did not end it and this I consider
to be an important point. Notwithstanding that these gentlemen did not grant what the farmers of these three provinces asked, the premier of Manitoba and Mr. Rutherford, of Alberta, did not think it well to allow the matter to drop there. They said: We cannot deal with this question, it would be unconstitutional, it is a matter for the Department of Trade and Commerce, it will have to be dealt with by the Dominion government. What did they do? I had Mr. Rutherford's resolution, but I am sorry to say that I cannot lay my hand on it at the moment, but I know that all western men will agree with me when I say that it was absolutely similar to the resolution introduced into the Manitoba legislature. Mr. Roblin thought he had better, make the matter public in that' country because he knew very well that these farmers are not to be put down. Here is the resolution that Mr. Roblin moved in the House within the last four weeks:
Resolved, that a memorial he presented to His Excellency the Governor in Council setting forth that:
Whereas the farmers of Manitoba are dissatisfied with the present arrangements for storing grain at initial points, the elevators being in the hands of the grain dealers;
And whereas, the farmers believe that it would be in their interests and in the interests of the public generally that the initial elevators be publicly owned and controlled;
And whereas, under our constitution the power to control and regulate the storage and handling, of grain, the weights and grades, the power to control and regulate the transportation companies and make the provision for the granting of elevator sites on railways, as well as the distribution of cars and generally all matters relating to the grain trade m Canada, rests in the federal parliament and not in the provinces, as provided in the British North America Act;
Therefore, this assembly begs to call Your Excellency's attention to the desirability of the government of Canada dealing with the initial elevator situation either by (a) making provision for government ownership and operation of the grain elevators in Manitoba-or (b) bv having conferred upon this province, either by Dominion or imperial legislation the power to fully deal with the question of storage transportation and grading of grain.	8
Perhaps the members of this House do not see the same signifiance in this resolution that I do, but I would like to say that practically the same resolution has been introduced into the Alberta House by the First Minister of that province. It is to me an indication of what I have seen coming for some time, and that is that these men think it is proper to get right with the farmers, and they are good politicians for seeing that.
What they are asking for was not only possible but was highly desirable in the interests of the grain growers of this country.

This is what Mr. Roblin says:
No utility or public service that has been taken over by any government and operated by them has been what has been called or is known as a monopoly, a public monopoly, such service as could best secure the convenience of it to the general public when in the form of a monopoly.

Under the provisions of the British North America Act it is specially provided that in all matters pertaining to trade and commerce the federal authorities shall be, and are, supreme. The fact that in holding or operating elevators it was requisite to weigh and to inspect grain put the proposition immediately in opposition to that portion of the British North American Act that refers to weights and measures and the inspection of grain. Further, under the general law, transportation companies, such as we have in this western country, are subject also to federal law.
In the event of the Dominion parliament failing to take that position, then the provinces would be justified in assuming functions they did not possess. ... We therefore felt that it is necessary for us, being in full sympathy with the purposes and objects the grain growers have in securing conditions that will secure them the fullest and largest measure of reward for their industry and their labour, to take such action as would indicate the position we have taken in this connection. I therefore move the resolution.
I do not think anything could be clearer, and I think it means a great deal that these three gentlemen who are in close touch with the farmers of that western country consider that this question is one of such importance that it is incumbent upon them to deal with it. They believe that these initial elevators are just as important as the terminal and transfer elevators. I do not need to tell our western men why, because they know all about it, but in order to make my argument as complete a3 I can make it, I would like for a moment Mr. SCHAFFNER.
to state how closely allied all these elevators are and how important they aTe to the farmer. The manufacturer and the railway man have problems to solve, but does any one present to-night imagine that the farmer has _ not greater problems to solve than any other class of our citizens? He has to decide how best to cultivate the soil, and like the manufacturer he has to meet strong competition whether it comes from his own or from a foreign country. True, only the fringe of the western prairie is yet cultivated, and, comparatively speaking, but a little patch of land here and there is under crop, but we grow 200,000,000 bushels of grain in Canada, and when cultivation extends over a larger area that production will be enormously increased. But the Canadian farmer has competition from Russia, which grows 500,000,000 bushels and from India, which grows 300,000,000 bushels, and from Argentine, which grows 200,000,000, and all that grain enters into competition in the British market with the grain grown by the farmers of Canada.
In view of this strenuous competition it is exceedingly important that the Canadian should be able to get his grain from the farmers* wagon to the British market under the most reasonable conditions. If he can save 2 cents per bushel it means $100 to the farmer who grows 5,000 bushels, and that will buy him a good suit of clothes, and his wife a pretty fair dress, and a good many pairs of boots for the children. You see how important then is this 2 cents a bushel saved at the elevator, or in the freight rates. No one denies that the great problem with the farmers' associations during the past two or three years has been the elevator question. Last year the interprovincial association sent three or delegates to Ottawa to meet in one of the most important conferences that was ever held here. That conference was held in the office of the Minister of Trade and Commerce with Sir Richard Cartwright ip the chair, and it was attended by repre-, sentatives of the railways, of the grain exchange, and of the banks and other financial institutions. The representatives of the farmers presented their case for terminal elevators, and it is not flattering them too much to say: that they held their own with the representatives of the other great institutions present. These representatives tried to get a condition of affairs which will enable the farmer to get the best possible price for his products under the keen competition which there will be in the world's market. The purpose I have m view is that the wheat as the farmer sells if from his farm shall arrive at the ultimate market in the condition in which he sells it. This can be accomplished only by full government control of internal term-

inal and transfer elevators. The farmers did not get exactly what they wanted; they never do at first; it is the man who keeps persistently at it who gets what he wants, and these farmers will keep persistently at it until they do get what they want. They know what they want and the people of eastern Canada will understand it when they take a little time to study the question. These farmers' delegates made a plea for government operation of terminal elevators and I quote from the pamphlet which was prepared by them:
We the undersigned members of the delegation representing the organized farmers of the three prairie provinces, at the request and on behalf of the whole delegation, beg to submit the following re-statement of the requests and recommendations made by us on behalf of our people at the conference held last week, with a view of putting them and the arguments advanced in their support, in a more orderly and concise form.
These farmers' delegates as I have said met with the members of the government and the representatives of the financial and transportation interests, and believing they did not get what they deserved, they prepared, after they returned home, the pamphlet from which I quote. It will be remembered that in the dying hours of last session at four o'clock in the morning some members of this House referred to the conference which had just been completed and they endeavoured to convince the government that the farmers of the west asked what was proper and fair:
At the outset it is proper that we should state whom we represent, the circumstances which led up to a delegation being appointed and our mission to Ottawa.
There are three large organizations of farmers in the west-the Grain Growers' Association of Manitoba, the Grain Grower's Association of Saskatchewan and the Alberta farmers' Association, the aggregate membership of which is in the neighborhood of ten thousand.
I would point out that the farmers are scattered throughout the west; the manufacturers are close together, and they have the impetus of contact which means a good deal in discussing any question. Supposing we had 10,000 farmers, and I would like to see it, marching up the street and taking their place in front of this building, then would the government of this country begin to realize that the farmers are a force in our national affairs. I hope the farmers of this country will never have to do that:
But we do not represent these alone. As the direct representatives of these ten thousand organized farmers who embrace the most intelligent and articulate portion of the farm population, we claim the right to be regarded as representatives of the whole body of western agriculturists.
Our presence as a delegation at Ottawa is the outcome of a conference of the representatives of the above mentioned farmers' associations which met at Saskatchewan last February and which after passing a number of important resolutions, arranged that two delegates should be sent from each association to press for the legislation required by these resolutions.
I think no one will deny that these gentlemen represented the sentiments of the western farmers as a whole:
We may add with respect to all the important resolutions passed at the conference, that they had been thoroughly discussed in approximate forms and agreed to by each of the provincial associations prior to being dealt with by the conference, so that most emphatically they represent the sentiments of the western farmers as a whole.
The resolution growing out of this asks that the Dominion government operate the transfer terminal elevators. Another resolution asks for the special binning of grains at the terminal elevators in order that a satisfactory market might be developed in Winnipeg for the common benefit of the farmer and the miller. I am not dealing to-night with the question of a sample market.
It is sometimes said that the farmers are not very definite in their requests and statement of grievances. I think their requests are definite. On four definite points which they believe to be grievances they are agreed: first, they believe that there is improper or too low grading of their wheat; second, they believe there is dishonest weighing; third, they believe there is excessive dockage, and fourth, they believe that there is loss of identity of 'the wheat. Any one familiar with the grain trade will realize that these are definite grievances. The hon. member for Regina (Mr. W. M. Martin) the other night referred to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway. If it would not be too much of a digression I would say that my position on the Grand Trunk is and always has been that we must have the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, we need it in that western country and no man can show that I have ever said anything to the contrary. The hon. member said that grain was being taken across the line, and I inferred from his statement that it was taken into the United States for transportation because it was not possible to secure transportation on the Canadian side. If that condition exists in Manitoba, it exists to a very limited extent. Our wheat is going across the border for quite a few miles north of the boundary although that movement was larger in the first part of the season than it was towards the last. Why was it going into the United States? Because it secured a better grade there than in Canada. Wheat that would grade in Boissevain, Waskada and Lyleton as No. 3 Northern

can get a No. 1 Northern under American grading.
The farmers are anxious to avoid the manipulation of their grain by these grain dealers who are always trying to make people believe that they have such tremendous interest in the farmer. Last year when the Roblin government introduced legislation in connection with the Winnipeg Grain Exchange, I happened to be in Winnipeg, and two of the first men I met, both pronounced Tories, spent two hours trying to convince me that the Roblin government had wronged the grain exchange, had ruined it. The Grain Exchange had commenced the erection of a great building and they said it would never be finished. What occurred? The Grain Exchange men fired off a little hot air, but it was not very long before they got together and the fine building went on and to-day the Grain Exchange is going on just as before. What does it mean? It means that when they could not fool the farmer in that particular respect they accepted what the farmer desired, and what was not absolutely against the interest of the Grain Exchange. The farmers believe that the only way in which their grievances and difficulties can be overcome is by having the whole system for the handling of the grain from the farmers' wagon to the markets of the world under the control of a staff of men who are not interested in the grain trade. They believe that the government should control the interior, terminal and transfer elevators, so that they may avoid injustice in reference to grades, weighing, dockage and the preservation of the identity of grain. If the government owned the internal elevators only, then when the grain reached the terminal elevators at the head of the lakes it would be mixed, there would be loss in weight and excessive dockage. I shall not deal tonight with the question of weight in relation to shipping between Port Arthur and the transfer elevators as I believe an hon. member who will follow me is far more familiar with that part of the question than I am. A very serious condition has arisen in connection with this link in the train of transportation. If the government controlled the elevators as far as the head of the lakes only, then the grain would leave the terminal elevators properly graded and unmixed, but the mischief would be done in the transfer elevators, so that the farmers are convinced that the only remedy is to have government control throughout the whole system. The farmers say with reference to that:	.
That the fact that our wheat is now received by eastern Canadian and British millers out of the terminals not cleaned as required by the Act, and sometimes showing evidence of being tampered with, although put out under the supervision of a government inspector,indicates that so long as those elevators are operated by parties who may Mr. SCHAFFNER.
profit by evading the provisions of the Act, no system of supervision can be relied on to prevent such practices nor in the light of such past experience, restore the public confidence.

Apart from the danger of friction between the operators and supervisors, the cost of maintaining two sets of employees where only one would be required under government operation, is a strong argument in favour of our contention.
What occurred after that convention of last year? The government did not give us what we asked, they did not say that they would operate the elevators-and the delegation did not ask the government to buy the elevators but to lease them to carry on the experiment for a few years. The government put on more inspectors, adding at Port Arthur and Fort William 25 additional men. That meant an unnecessary number of men to be paid ultimately out of the price of the wheat. It will be seen at once that under this system two set of men are employed to do the work that one set of men could do. The grain dealer will have his set of men and there is also the government staff, and no matter by whom they are employed, these men have to be paid out of the price of the wheat. Then we have perhaps too many elevators. I do not know whether that statement will be accepted by this House, but that nevertheless is the case. It may not exist to such an extent in the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta, but it certainly exists to some extent in Manitoba. An ordinary elevator can take care of about 150,000 bushels of grain during the season. Every little town in Manitoba-take for instance Miami-will have about four or five elevators. Well, if one elevator can take care of 150,000 bushels of grain, the strong probability is that three out of the four or five elevators in Miami last year did not handle more than about 30,000 bushels each. Nevertheless, each one has to keep its full staff of officers and it costs just as much to maintain it as if it handled 150,000 bushels. If that condition of affairs exists, it must add to the cost of transporting our grain, and the way to avoid that would be by government control. If we had government control, we would have just sufficient elevators in one town to take care of the grain shipped from that town and just sufficient men employed to take care of these elevators. Every one who has lived in the western provinces knows how the business is done. A farmer comes in with a load of grain.. If there are five or six elevators in the town, there are five or six men on the street. They run out to meet the farmer. They jump on to hi3 wagon and make a grade; and 90 times out of a 100, the grade which the first man puts on the wheat is the grade that goes,

and the price which the first man offers is the price that goes. Only about two years ago, I believe there was a pooling system, and one of the results of this conference was to do away with that system. If we have in all these towns too many elevators and too many men employed, we are put to too much expense and we can lessen that expense by having one control of the wheat, by having a man to weigh and grade and ship our wheat, who has absolutely no interest in it. To-day a man takes the wheat off the farmer's wagon at a low grade. Perhaps he pays the farmer for grade three. Then he mixes that wheat with other wheat grade number one or two, and sells it for grade number one. It makes of course quite a difference to the farmer whether he gets paid for grade one or grade three. In that country we get very little number one hard. The great bulk of the grain last year was number one northern or number two northern.
