Only government operation and government control of our wheat from the time it leaves our wagons until it reaches the British market will bring about the result we have the right to desire to reach in connection with the selling of wheat.
Now, Sir, I had no idea of taking up so much time with this question, but as I said in the beginning, I have no apology to make, for the governments of this country will very soon have to recognize and deal with this question of elevators. The elevator is the proper _ way of handling wheat. We have the privilege of loading wheat directly on the cars; we have our car platforms all over the country. But the most convenient way to transfer our grain is to transfer it through these elevators.
There is another point that I forgot to mention, and I will mention it now, because I think it will give some information to this House of a useful character. As a matter of fact we only shipped about 78,000,000 bushels of wheat last year, and we have in this country internal and transfer elevators to the capacity of 75,000,000 bushels. We do not need as much elevator capacity as we can grow grain, that is self-evident to anybody. I want to say that these terminal elevators at Fort William and Port Arthur, with the exception of the elevators owned by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, are owned and operated by private companies. The Canadian, Pacific Railway Company has three elevators at Port Arthur and three elevators at Fort William, with a capacity of 7,777,700 bushels. At Keewatin, the Lake of the Woods Milling Company has one elevator and the Lake of the Woods Manufacturing Company has one. At Port Arthur, Joseph G. King & Co. have a terminal elevator There we have five elevators with a capacity of over
13,000,000 bushels. The Canadian Northern has two elevators at Port Arthur with a capacity of over 7,000,000 bushels. These are terminal elevators. Then we have transfer elevators, and there are more of them than I supposed. At Kingston the Canadian Pacific Railway have an elevator of the capacity of 500,000 bushels, the Montreal
Transportation Company have one with a capacity of 761,000; James Richardson & Son have one with a capacity of 235,000, or a total of 996,000 bushels. Then the Grand Trunk-I am not giving all'the figures-at Collingwood, Depot Harbour, Meaford, Midland, Prescott and Tiffin have seven elevators with a capacity of 7,000,000 bushels. Of eastern transfer elevators, there are three at Montreal with a capacity of about
2.500.000.	The Canadian Northern has at Quebec four elevators with a capacity of about 3,000,000. The Canadian Pacific Railway have an elevator in St. John with a capacity of 1,000,000. The Intercolonial has one at St. John with a capacity of 500,000; one at Halifax with a capacity of 500,000; total, three elevators with a capacity of
2.000.	000. Now, we have in Manitoba 689 elevators with a capacity of over 20,000,000 bushels; Saskatchewan has 615 elevators with a capacity of about 18,000,000 bushels; Alberta has 109 elevators with a capacity of 4,000,000 bushels, totalling over 43,000,000 bushels. Adding the Ontario terminals with a capacity of over 20,000,000 bushels, we have a total capacity in the western division of 63,190,000. Adding those in the eastern division we have, as I have said, a total capacity of 78,000,000 bushels.
When we consider the amount of capital that is invested in these elevators, is it not about time that we had some better system of running the business? Does anybody in this House pretend to tell me that the manufacturers or the railway men would conduct their business in this way? What have the manufacturers of this country been doing for years in order to meet competition? They have tried to manufacture with less expense; they have tried to get better results from the labour employed, and we find combinations formed. We find the Massey Company and the Harris Company combined into the Massey-Harris Company. I am well acquainted with these companies and have known them a good many years. Thev found that by bringing their men and plants together they could manufacture more machinery, and perhaps better machinery, and could manufacture it cheaper. Now, as we grow more grain in the west we shall need more elevator capacity. Wheat is bringing a good price now, and we do not feel the need of these things quite so much. When the farmer gets $1 a bushel for his wheat he doesn't do quite so much kicking if he has to pay a little more. Everybody in the west has been getting that price for the last couple of yeaTS. But for many years previously the farmer sold his wheat'at a price that barely paid expenses. Who knows but what that condition of affairs may come again. In all probability it will come. Then I say that now is the time, when things are prosperous ! and prices are good, that we should set to

work and try to regulate and improve the present condition of affairs in the best interest of the farmers. I say that this elevator question is just as important as any railway question, and I ask the government to give the matter their careful consideration. The farmers deserve it. It would pay our great financial centres, it would pay Montreal, St. John, Toronto and every other city to give this matter their consideration. While eastern Canada is a very important part of confederation, everybody admits that if Canada is going to become a great nation it depends upon the west. At some future time we may have to go into mixed farming, and perhaps dairying; but to-day, and for a number of years to come, the great industry of that country will be the growing of wheat. Consequently it becomes of the utmost importance that we .should get our wheat to the market as cheaply as possible. Nine-tenths of the products of the soil that we export in Canada go to the British markets. What are we doing as legislators? We are sent here by the farmers to look after their interests, and it is our duty to see that they get their products to the foreign markets under the best possible conditions and at the lowest possible rates. In conclusion, I believe that a tax of li cents or 11 cents per bushel for grain going through an elevator would pay the cost of operation, pay the interest on bonds necessary to purchase the present system and also create a sinking fund which would pay the bonds off when they come due. I ask the government to give this matter their very serious consideration, and if they can help the farmers in any way they will not only be benefiting them, but the whole country.

I have said enough to prove the first part of the resolution, that the present system is detrimental to the western grain producers. The second part of the resolution reads:
That the government should take immediate steps to operate terminal elevators at Port William and Port Arthur, and the transfer elevators between these terminals and the Atlantic sea-board.
I take it, that we are first likely to be met with objection on the score of expense, but that objection can only be urged by those who have not closely studied the question. To my mind there will be no expense whatever incurred. The fees charged for having grain inspected by the public inspectors usually meets the whole cost of that inspection so far as the western part of the inspection is concerned. In addition to that there will be the cost of operating, but that comes out of the grain itself now, and it will so continue if the government take charge of the operation. The government will still charge probably very much the same fees which are now charged by the private corporations, but the cost of inspection will be saved. The system of government operation should be and would be self-supporting, and would be no charge whatever on the country.
A second objection which may be urged by the government is the old stock objection, the question of government ownership. In this connection I would point out that the government already is the owner of a transfer elevator at Port Colborne and as the proprietors of the Intercolonial Railway, they own elevators at some of the eastern ocean ports. In addition to that I would point out that through the Prime Minister the government have made a definite promise when the Hudson Bay Railway is completed the government will build and own and keep under their own ownership the terminals and the elevators which will be erected at the Hudson Bay port. The Prime Minister, as it will be clearly remembered, made a great speech at Niagara in the early part of the recent campaign That speech was considered and treated by speakers throughout Canada as the great exposition of the policy which the government was prepared to carry into effect if they were returned to power. It has already been quoted in the House by the Minister oi Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) as a statement of what the policy of the government will be in one respect, and I have no doubt whatever that it will be confirmed by other members of the government as an exposition of the government's policy in regard to the ownership of terminal elevators at the Hudson's Bay port. Speaking at Niagara on September 16, 1908, Mr. LAKE.
Sir Wilfrid Laurier is thus reported in The 'Globe':	Speaking of the Hudson's Bay
railway, he said:
The government will build the railway or rather somebody will be entrusted with the building but whatever we do, all the terminals and all the elevators shall be built by the government and retained, under all circumstances, by the government so as ,to ensure the largest measure of benefit possible to the Canadian people in the northwest provinces.
There is a most definite and distinct promise of government ownership and operation of the elevators which are to be constructed on the shores of Hudson bay and so the Prime Minister and head of the government having adopted the principle of government ownership in connection with terminal elevators at one ocean port, surely he cannot see any insuperable difficulty in adopting the same principle in regard to terminal elevators and transfer elevators at other ports. It would be only an expansion of the system which they themselves proposed of their own volition to carry into effect in the Hudson bay, and it would certainly be an anomaly to have the government adopting one system on the Hudson bay and a miscellaneous series of systems in other parts of the Dominion. There would, I think, be no objection on the part of the present elevator owners. We had that from the mouths of some of them who gave evidence* before the Minister of Trade ana Commerce at the conference which took place last year. The great transportation companies, I think, would actually welcome the government coming in and operating their elevators. Their great fear in connection with this increased system of inspection was that the dual system of control would probably be an obstacle in the way of the efficient and speedy operation of the elevators. I was personally told by a representative of the railways who was then present that he would be very glad to see the government step in and operate all these elevators so long as they did it efficiently, and I think there ought to be very little difficulty in having an efficient administration at any rate of an elevator system by the government. A gentleman who attended that conference representing the Winnipeg grain exchange and also representing the owners of some of these private-owned terminal elevators at lake ports, stated that there would be no objection so far as he could see to the government taking these elevators over and operating them; in fact the impression made on my mind by his evidence was that these private corporations would welcome government operation. I am quite confident, to sum up this matter, that there would be no objection to it on the part of the trans-

portation companies and there should be no objection on the part of the grain exporting companies who intend to do a legitimate business, and the objections of those who do not intend to do a legitimate business I do not think should be considered. The action called for is the corollary of the position which is taken by the government in the matter of grading and inspection, it is the logical sequence to the inspection by the government of all grain, and the granting of government certificates, that the grain should remain under the absolute control and in the hands of government officers so long as it remains within the borders of the Dominion and until it is placed on the ocean-going steamers. That seems to be the logical sequence of our system of grading and certificating grain.
I believe, as I have said that the whole business would be self-supporting. It would cost no more than the present system, in fact it would be a less costly system as it would be all under the government operation and the fees charged at the present time would more than cover the whole cost. No burden whatever would be placed on the government in carrying the system through.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure that all members of the House appreciate the very great importance of the subject that has been brought to our attention by the hon. members for Souris (Mr. Schaffner) and Qu'Appelle (Mr. Lake). We are aware that the grain question is of prime importance to the western Canadian farmer. Whatever other products may be raised, we must all recognize this fact that wheat is, par excellence, the product of western Canada. We are all aware of the enormous amount to which the production of grain, and particularly of wheat and the coarser grains, has increased throughout the three prairie provinces. In the province of Saskatchewan, from which I come, the production this last year was in round numbers over 100,000,000 bushels of coarser grains, of which over 50,000,000 bushels was wheat. In Manitoba the amount was somewhat smaller. In Alberta the grain growing industry has not been developed to the same extent, but the amount each year is rapidly increasing. We therefore can all . appreciate the great importance to the western farmers of everything which has any bearing on the price of their chief commodity. I have before me some statistics furnished by the Department of Trade and Commerce, in its weekly report of March 15, 1909, which show how rapidly the production of grain is increasing in western Canada. For the six months ending in February of this year, from September, 1908, to end of February, 1909, the total amount of grain received in the terminal elevators at Fort William and Port Arthur was something over 60,000,000 bushels. For the same period in 1907-8 the amount was a little under 40,000,000 bushels. So that in one year alone, we have increased the amount of grain shipped in these corresponding periods of six months 50 per cent.
Of course anything which affects the price of wheat must necessarily be of great interest to the western grower, and any movement made in this House or outside it for the purpose of procuring to the western farmers a proper price for their grain must have the cordial sympathy and support of this House, especially of representatives from the west of Lake Superior. There is equally no doubt that the farmers of western Canada are not content with the present conditions surrounding the grain trade, rot only as regards the export of grain, by the terminal and transfer elevators at Fort William and eastwards, but also as regards the purchase of grain from the farmers' wagons. The greatest loss to the western Canadian producer does not come from the operations of the terminal elevators at Fort William and Port Arthur and the transfer elevator further east but from the very great spread between what are commonly known as track and street wheat. Ever since our farmers have had the privilege of getting their own cars and shipping direct their own wheat, a condition prevails under which the small farmer, who is compelled to sell by the v\ agon load on the street, gets a very iarge margin less than the farmer who loads his own car and ships direct to the terminal elevators. The reason given by the elevator companies for this disparity is the great difficulty they experience in getting sufficient cars from the transportation companies to ship out the grain when they want to ship it. They say that when they purchase a wagon load, they do not know when they will get a car to ship it in, and for this they blame the car distribution clause of the Manitoba Act. Therefore, they say, they must sell for a future market and not the market that obtains at the moment, and for that reason have to allow a reasonable spread between the price' of street wheat and that of track wheat. To my mind the greatest loss that comes to the farmer does not come from the operations of the terminal or transfer elevators referred to in the resolution, but from the very great spread between the price of the street and the track wheat in the country town where the farmer brings his wheat either for sale or shipment, and I cannot understand why this resolution did not include a recommendation that the government should also take over the interior elevators. If they are going to do the thing at all, why not do it entirely? Therefore., while my sympathy is strongly with any movement tending to enhance the price of wheat to the farmer and give him proper remuneration for his toil, I do not think that the

resolution submitted by my hon. friend from Souris (Mr. Schaffner) would by any means combat all the evils, or even the most important, which the farmer has to contend with. I am quite aware that the Grain Growers' Associations of Manitoba and Saskatchewan and the Farmers' Association of Alberta have made certain representations to this government. One of these is that the government should take over the terminal elevators at Fort William and Port Arthur and the transfer elevators further east. So far as the principle involved is concerned, I have no serious objection to offer except this. Canada is a young country and these large elevator interests have vested rights in this country. They have established themselves at Fort William and Port Arthur, they have established transfer elevators further east, and I would like to call the attention of the mover and seconder of this resolution to a series of practical difficulties. They have established these transfer elevators, and I would call the attention of the mover and seconder of this resolution to the fact that there is a serious practical difficulty in the way. Suppose the government did accept this proposition, what should they do? Should they lease these elevators? The owners might not be willing to lease them. Should they expropriate them? That would be a very radical measure to take. Suppose they were to construct opposition terminal and transfer elevators, how would the capitalists all over the world, to whom a young country like Canada must look for necessary capital to carry on great industrial operations, view such a step on the part of the government? I am not objecting to this resolution now, but I am calling attention to this practical difficulty, which, apparently, these hon. gentlemen have not thought of, which, at least, they have not discussed.
The hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Lake) stated that the leader of the government had told the people that when the government of this country built the road to Hudson bay it was their purpose to own and operate the terminals there. That is a very much simpler proposition. There are no terminal elevators there now, and so there will be no vested interests established through the investment of private capital to be affected by these governmental terminal elevators. It would be quite reasonable to ask the government to undertake such a work, and one which we of western Canada are glad the leader of the government has promised the people of the west he will undertake in the immediate future. It strikes me as a very peculiar thing that according to the statements of these hon. gentlemen no system of government control or supervision of these terminals and transfer elevators could successfully meet the difficulties of the western Canadian farmers who think there is manipulation of the Mr. NEELY.
grain passing through them. We had a case of an investigation of the practices of terminal elevators at Duluth, and how these elevators manipulate the grain that came from the producers of the western states; so that, whereas a large amount of wheat of low grade went into these elevators, when it was shipped out all these low grades were found to have disappeared and nothing but high grades were shipped. Surely this House is not asked to believe that these elevators were under a system of government supervision such as the terminal elevators at Fort William and Port Arthur? I am willing to admit that the .farmers of the west have had serious objections to these terminal elevators. One of the strongest objections is that the corporations that operate the majority of these terminal elevators are those interested in the grain trade further back-that is men who are back of the corporations hold elevators at different points along the great lines of railway throughout the three provinces. The contention of the farmers is that on account of these grain dealers having control of the terminal elevators they are in a position to manipulate the grain that passes through and to carry on practices similar to those described as having been carried on in the terminal elevators at Duluth. I admit that the evidence taken before the Grain Commission appointed by this government in 1906 did give support to that suspicion in the minds of the western Canadian farmers. As a result of that commission and its report, and as a result of the inquiry and report made last session, the Department of Trade and Commerce, I understand, has increased the number of officers in the terminal elevators at Fort William, I believe bv twenty-five men. Yet the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Schaffner) tells us that the management of the grain that passes through these elevators is not satisfactory; that wheat shipped out of lots inspected by the grain inspector at Winnipeg, and graded No. 1 Northern, were received at certain points in Ontario and were found to be only No. 2 or No. 3 northern. I cannot understand how such a thing could possibly oocur, if the inspectors at Fort William and Port Arthur are doing their work as it ought to be done. If these things are true, to my mind there should be a thorough investigation, and if these men representing the government are doing their work in an unsatisfactory way, it is time we had a change in the government officials at these points. There might be an isolated instance, but if this is a common occurrence it is time for an investigation into the methods of our officials. While I am not opposing this resolution, I think that the nresent system at Fort William and Port Arthur ought to be given a fair trial. It has had just one year of

operation, and we cannot very well judge of a system of this kind as the result of one year. I think we should be careful in adopting a resolution of .this kind, one which, if carried out, entails very serious practical difficulties. Especially should we be careful about advocating this system before we have given the existing system of government supervision a fair trial. I maintain that that system has not had a fair trial; one year is not a sufficient time, and that an isolated instance such as given by the hon. member for Souris when he referred to this grain shipped from the elevators in the month of January and found to be of lower grade is not a sufficient reason why the government should take this important step.
Now in 1906 this government appointed a Royal Commission to investigate the grain trade. Here I want to say that we must not be led by the remarks that have been made here to-night in support of this resolution, to think that all the farmers of the west are agreed on the proposition that the government should own and operate the terminal elevators at Fort William and Port Arthur and further east; because, as far as my opinion goes, there is a great diversity of opinion on that question. I want just to read from the last page of the report of the Royal Commission on the Grain Trade of Canada to confirm what I have said; I want to read the conclusions that were arrived at after thorough investigation of this subject by the Royal Commission. After stating that they found the terminal elevators at Port Arthur and Fort William were largely in the hands of private companies, this report goes on to say:
8.	We believe the operating of terminal elev-vators by private companies under the present regulations would be detrimental to the interests of the trade, and would tend to destroy public confidence in the results obtained therefrom. Our reasons for believing this are, that the elevator companies (if they so wish) would be able to manipulate the grades for their own benefit and not to clean grain up for the dockage set by the government inspector.
9.	The fact that an elevator is owned and operated by a railway company does not with the present regulations, in our opinion, necessarily ensure protection to the public. We would like, however, to see the elevators at present owned, or to be owned, by the railways operated by them.
10.	To prevent the evils that are made possible by the operation of terminal elevators under the present system, we do not think it wise to advise the government to go to the length of taking over the terminal elevators or of prohibiting persons engaged in the grain trade bein" interested in such terminals. We believe it is possible to obtain a good service from these elevators under the present ownership ibv having a more thorough system of supervision and control.
This report is signed by John Miller, W.
L.	MacNair and George E. Goldie, the
three commissioners who were appointed to investigate the grain trade. They went thoroughly into the whole question, and their view is that the radical step-or what seems so to many of us-of the government taking over all the terminal and transfer elevators from Fort William eastward, is not one on which the western farmers are unanimous. This commission also recommended, as you have noticed, a more thorough supervision and control on the part of the government to meet the needs of the grain trade so far as these terminal and transfer elevators are concerned. I may say that as a result of this investigation into the grain trade of the west, and as a result of their report, and the investigation into the report held last year, some important improvements were made to the Manitoba Grain Act, and some amendments were made to the Inspection and Sale Act that met at least a part of the objections of the farmers to the way in which the grain trade had been handled previous to that time. But I am free to say that there are still some serious handicaps on the grain trade in the way in which it is handled from Fort William eastward. One of the things that is harmful to the grain trade of the west and to the producer, one of the conditions that is injurious, is met by the vessels employed in the carrying trade on the great lakes. When they carry grain from Chicago, ot from Duluth, or from ports on the American side, they find at those points, established by the grain trade itself, clearing houses where a vessel can go to one elevator, or to two or three at most, and obtain a full cargo of grain. As a result of these clearing houses for documents at those ports on the American side, a vessel can go to one of those ports and take a load of grain in a few hours, not exceeding in any case half a day. What is the condition of affairs at Port Arthur and Fort William? In a place where they have a dozen terminal elevators, in order to get her cargo a vessel has to go from one to another, she has to go around six or seven, or eight elevators before she has obtained her ioad. That means, not a matter of a few hours, but a matter of two or three days, in many cases; that means a great increase in the cost of carrying this grain, because the owners of these vessels cannot afford, when so much time is lost in loading the grain, to charge the same freight rates from Fort William as they do from corresponding ports on the American side. Now I think the government should require the grain trade that is interested in these terminal elevators at Fort William and Port Arthur, to establish a clearing house for documents whereby a vessel could go to one or two elevators and receive her cargo, and the other elevators interested could use this elevator as a clearing house for the quantity that

they propose to ship. That could easily be done, that would be an easy matter to accomplish, and I think that would remove one of the very serious sources of loss to the producer of western Canadian wheat. Then again the mover and seconder of this resolution have referred to the fact that when these vessels, that are loaded at Fort William and Port Arthur, where the grain is weighed into them by a government weighmaster, reach the Georgian bay and other eastern ports, in many cases very serious shortages are found, and of course the carrying trade refuse to be responsible for those shortages. That again is another slap in the face for the producer of western Canadian wheat. I think there is another instance where the government might do a little something in the interest of the grain trade. It seems to me that if we are to have an effective system, if we are going to have men to weigh out this grain into the vessels at Fort William and Port Arthur, we should also have government weighmasters to weigh this grain into the eastern transfer elevators, and in that way another source of loss to the producer in the west would be removed. In my opinion the grain trade of western Canada is one of absorbing interest and importance, and when we come to consider the amount of grain that is being produced, and that will be produced in those prairie provinces the next few years, anything that will effect a saving to the farmer of a cent a bushel, or half a cent, or even a quarter of a cent, or of a less fraction than that, means the saving of a large sum of money to the people of western Canada.
The farmer works hard, as we know, for his living. He earns his bread by the sweat of his brow, literally, and I maintain that everything that can be done by this government and the House to lighten the burden of the western Canadian farmer, to bring to him a fair and just reward of the toil that is necessary for the production of grain, of wheat, oats and other cereals on our western farms, ought to be done. I am sure that the members of the government who are listening to me do so with sympathetic interest. The farmers of the west appreciate very much what the government have already done along this line. We know that last year, when the farmers interviewed upon this grain question the right hon. the Minister of Trade and Commerce, there were very powerful interests present at that interview, and that these other interests sought in every way possible to influence this government to abolish certain provisions of the Manitoba Grain Act which were in the farmers' interests. I say that it is to the credit of this government that they did not listen to these other powerful interests, but that they listened to the voice of the western Canadian farm-Mr. NEELY.
ers. It would have been a great calamity to the western farmer if the car distribution clause had been altered. I hope the government, even if they do not see their way clear to adopt the resolution of the hon. member for Souris, will manifest a sympathetic interest, as they have done in the past, in the representations made by the people of western Canada in connection with everything necessary to improve and promote the welfare of the grain trade of the west. In conclusion I have to say that I quite agree with the view that government supervision and control should follow the farmers' wheat from the time it is taken off the railway car at Winnipeg or Fort William right through to the Atlantic seaboard. A complete and efficient system of control and supervision should be established, as it has been at Fort William and Port Arthur, in connection with the transfer elevators farther east. If that system is given a fair trial and if it is put into effective working order, if this supervision which has been brought into force as far as the terminal elevators at Fort William and Port Arthur are concerned, is extended to the eastern transfer elevators, so as to see that the identity of the farmers' grain, as it is shipped from his own town, is preserved right through to the Atlantic seaboard, the farmers of the west will be very well satisfied with the condition of affairs that will be brought about by this increased supervision and improved control.

I did not intend to take any part in this discussion and I do not intend to detain the House at any great length at this late hour. I thought when the hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Neely) rose1- to address this House that I would Rave been able to have congratulated the west on being united on this very important question. There is no doubt that this is a very important question to the west and every argument that the hon. gentleman has used here to-night in sunnort of a better system of supervision at the terminal elevators has, I think, been a very strong argument in support of the resolution before the House for government-ownership of the terminal elevators. I do not intend to detain the House. Everything I might say would simply be a repetition of what has been so well said by the mover and seconder of this resolution. There is no doubt that something ought to be done to protect the farmer, to make it possible that the grain that he ships from the great provinces of the west would Teach the markets of the world in the condition in which it leaves those provinces. The information that we have had laid before us to-night and the information that every man from the west has had time and again placed before him proves conclusively that the grain has been tampered with at the elevators en route to market and that the

grain that leaves the western provinces does not reach the consumer in the British market in the condition in which it leaves. This is a very important question not only for the farmers of the west, but for the whole of Canada. We have the reputation of raising the finest grain in the world, and I believe there is no question that we deserve that reputation. Manitoba and the other two great provinces of the west are producing to-day a sample of grain that has no equal in the world and it is the duty of the government to see that from the time it leaves the farmer until it reaches the consumer in the old land it is not tampered with. In conclusion, I had hoped that the west would be united in support of this resolution. I was a little surprised to hear the argument advanced by the hon. member for Humboldt, and I was surprised that he should desire to throw any obstacle in the way of a resolution of this kind. But, while he did not wish to come out openly and oppose this resolution, he went on to say that what the government had done and were doing was sufficient for the present and that the present system of government-supervision should be given a further trial. I do not know what the government are accomplishing upon these lines, but I say that anything that will improve the condition of the farmer and make it possible for his wheat to reach the markets of the world in a better condition than it does at the present time ought to be supported by every hon. member from the great west. I have much pleasure in concurring in the resolution which has been so ably presented by the hon. member for Souris, and seconded by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle. The information that has been laid before this House ought to convince every man in the House, if it has not succeeded in convincing the hon. member for Humboldt, of the necessity of doing something along these lines. I hope the time is coming when the government will take action. I regret very much that the provincial governments could not see their way clear to do something in the way of taking over the internal elevators. There is no doubt that there have been very serious complaints made as to the manner in which the farmers have been treated by these elevators. But they have, in their wisdom, decided that they have no power to do this and in fact thev have stated practically that it belongs to this parliament to take action in this matter. I can only say that I had hoped that the government would have accepted and made this a government measure, and I am sure that every man coming from the west would have been glad to have seen the resolution accepted and put through in that way. I trust that the speakers who will follow me from the other side of the House-because there are a number of them who are better qualified to speak on this question than I
am-will support the resolution moved by my hon. friend from Souris and seconded by my right hon. friend from Qu'Appelle.

Mr. Speaker, like other hon. members who have spoken in regard to this subject, I want to state that I thoroughly agree that it is of the utmost importance not only to the farmers of western Canada but also the business men, professional men and inhabitants generally of that western country.
If by any legislation that can be passed in this House changing the present method of handling grain, an additional return is obtainable by the producers of western grain, then the whole Dominion of Canada will be benefited. When we consider that the production of grain in the w>est is only in its infancy and that if is almost impossible to estimate the vast quantity which can be produced in that country, and when we consider that part of that western country is wholly dependent upon the production of wheat and other grain, it must be admitted that this question is of great importance not alone to the people of western Canada but to the people of the east. Now, referring to the question of government ownership which is included * in the motion of my hon. friend (Mr. Schaffner) I have to say that taking government ownership as a general principle I am opposed to it. But, if it can be shown that under the present system of government control there is dishonest weighing at the terminal elevators at Fort William and Port Arthur, and that grades are being manipulated, and if these abuses should continue to exist after the system of government control has been given a fair chance I would most certainly support government ownership in the interests of the grain producing industry of the west.
I congratulate the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Schaffner) on the manner in which he presented his case to the House, but it does seem to me that he offered no conclusive argument in favour of government ownership as compared with government control. I was not able to gather from the remarks of the hon. gentleman that the defects existed at the terminal elevators of Fort William and Port Arthur, because when he began to find fault with the system he went back to the small country elevators and said that the fault lay there. He spoke of the improper grading of the grain, but where is it graded? So far as I know it is graded at Winnipeg, and I do not see how you can get over improper grading at Winnipeg by adopting a policy of government ownership of terminals at Fort William and Port Arthur. The hon. gentleman spoke of dishonest weights, but I take it that this and other evils are provided against in the amendment to the Manitoba

Grain Act and to the Inspection and Sale Act which were passed by parliament last year. I claim that government control if properly carried out should be as efficient as government ownership, if not more so. Under the present system you have two sets of officials, the government officials and the employees of the terminal elevators, who act as a check upon each other. But if the elevators were owned and operated by the government there would be only one set of officials to weigh in the grain and to weigh it out, so that the present system if properly carried out ought to give us more efficient control than the system of government ownership. I had expected that the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Schaffner) and the hon. member for Qu'Ap-pelle (Mr. Lake) would give us some concrete instances of the success of government ownership, but in that I was disappointed. No doubt there are cases in which government ownership has been a success but there are many instances in which it has been a failure, and if we look at the examples of government ownership in this country we all have to admit that there is not much comfort for us in the prospect. One of the main arguments against government ownership is that it interferes more or less with individual enterprise, and the moment a government steps into that field it is going beyond what is the primary function of government. A government, is intended primarily to legislate and to administer; it is not its function to engage in private enterprise. I hold that the system of government control has not yet been given a fair trial because the Act only came into force on the 1st of September, 1908, and only one crop has been handled under it. I would advocate giving that system a fair chance to work out, and if it is not effective no doubt amendments can be made to the legislation which will make it effective. I believe that so far as terminal elevators are concerned, government ownership should only be adopted as a last resort and after it has been demonstrated that government control will not protect the grain producers of the west. The last part of the resolution moved by my hon. friend would seem to be all right if we once admit the principle of government ownership, but, I cannot at all agree with the first part of the resolution which says:
That in the opinon of the House the present system of operating terminal and transfer elevators is detrimental to the interests of western grain producers.
In the year 1906 we had a grain commission consisting of three prominent western men who followed the grain from the time it was harvested and threshed until it reached the Liverpool market, and that Mr. W. M. MARTIN.
commission presented a report to the government. Following the presentation of that report all the grain interests of the west were represented before the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and as a consequence of the conference then held certain amendments were made last session to the Manitoba Grain Act and to the Inspection and Sale Act, all of which amendments were in the interests of the western grain producers. I therefore cannot subscribe to the first part of that resolution which is in reality a criticism of the legislation passed by the government last session, and which legislation, was, I say, in the interest of the western grain producers. I referred a moment ago to the report of the Grain Commission. As I stated that commission followed the course of the grain from the thresher to the Liverpool market. They made certain recommendations to the government, among them the recommendation referred to by the hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Neely) that they did not believe it would be to the advantage of. the grain trade that the government should take over the terminal elevators at Port Arthur and Fort William. At page 9 of their report they say:
Requests were made of us in the country that the elevators at Fort William and Port Arthur should be taken over and operated by the government in view of the fact that so many of them were operated by private corporations interested in the grain trade. We also had a communication from the department, under date January 23, 1907, inclosing a petition of members of parliament addressed to the right hon. the Prime Minister, requesting that we be instructed specifically to inquire into and report whether it is in the public interest that terminal elevators continue to be operated by common carriers or allowed to pass into the hands of or be operated by persons, firms or corporations engaged in the grain business.
In reply to this communication we addressed to the Rt. Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright, Minister of Trade and Commerce, a letter dated February 1, 1907, a copy of which is appended hereto. We can see no reason for changing the conclusions arrived at at that time, and we believe that if our recommendations are carried out they will give to the public the same confidence and protection in the operation of these elevators as if they were owned ,by the government.
The communication addressed to Sir Richard Cartwright was referred to by the hon. member for Humboldt. The commissioners refer to it on page 19 of their report and say that they had no reason at the time they drew up their report to change their opinion with respect to the government ownership of terminal elevators at Fort William and Port Arthur. That is the view of the three men appointed by the government to investigate the conditions of the grain trade; they reported that they were not in favour of government ownership of terminal ele-vatoTs and did not think it would be in the '

interest of the trade to have the elevators taken over and operated by the government.
As I understand, the main objection that can be raised to the present method of handling the terminal elevators at Fort William or Port Arthur is that except the' Canadian Pacific Railway elevator they are either leased or owned by private companies engaged in the grain trade. The element of personal gain, of illegitimate gain in some cases, enters into the operation of these elevators, and if we can get some legislation in addition to what we have, eliminating that element of personal gain, I believe we will go a long way towards securing what is desired as to terminal facilities at Fort William and Port Arthur. The commissioners in their report refer to these elevators being owned in this way and I have some evidence here which goes to show that the grain coming out of the Canadian Pacific Railway elevator and going towards the eastern transfer elevators is in better condition than that from private company-owned elevators. The secretary of the Dominion Millers' Association, under date of January 9, 1909, communicated with the Department of Trade and Commerce as follows:
There is a marked difference in the quality of the grain coming out of privately owned or operated terminal elevators as compared with the Canadian Pacific Railway elevators. Both dealers and millers tell me that the wheat out of the Canadian Pacific Railway elevator is on an average one-half to one cent a bushel, and sometimes the difference is considerably greater, better value than out of elevators owned or operated by companies interested in buying and selling grain. All the terminal elevators except those owned by the Canadian Pacific Railway are operated by men dealing in grain and largely controlled by United States concerns and managed by experts from across the line.
That bears out what I said in regard to private gain entering into the management of the elevators at Fort William and Port Arthur, the evidence going to show that the Canadian Pacific Railway elevator put out their grain in better shape than the el"eva; tors operated and owned by private corporations.
To refer again to the report of the grain commissioners, in their letter to Sir Richard Cartwright in the year 1907 they practically bear out what is stated by the Dominion Millers' Association, because they say the terminal elevators would be operated in a better way and more in the interests of the grain producers of the west if they were handled by the transportation companies. Apart from the question of government ownership altogether, there is a method of getting free from this element of personal gain, which will continue as long as human nature exists as it is, for the grain men are not in the business for nothing, they are in it to make as much money as they can. Why should not legislation be passed providing that no warehouse man at either
point should be engaged in the grain business, simply make him a warehouse man pure and simple, or instead of that provide that the railway companies must not only build elevators but operate and own them. Take away the element of personal private gain from these elevators, take away from the grain men the gain derived from manipulating the grain in the terminals and I think it will go a long way towards eliminating the difficulties now existing in the handling of grain.
I have referred to the legislation passed last year. I claim that if this legislation is properly enforced under the system of government control, it must remove the difficulties of mixing grades which are alleged to exist at these terminal elevators. For instance, we find in the Act to amend the Manitoba Grain Act of last year, chapter 45 of the statutes of 1908, section 10, the following:
2.	Every public terminal elevator warehouseman in the Manitoba inspection division shall receive for storage any grain tendered to him in a dry and suitable condition for warehousing, in the usual manner in which terminal elevators are accustomed to receive grain in the ordinary and usual course of business. ,
3.	Grain so received shall in all cases be inspected and graded by a duly authorized inspector, and shall be stored with grain of a similar grade.
4.	No grain shall leave a public terminal point without being officially weighed, unless the owner or his agent orders otherwise.
The Act then speaks of a record to be kept of this grain, and then refers to the preservation of the identity of the grain, the clause reading:
The identity of each parcel or lot of western grain shipped to an eastern transfer elevator shall be preserved, except that different parcels or lots of the same grades may be binned together when there is not sufficient space in the elevator to keep the parcels or lots separate,
8. In no case, whether in a pub'io terminal elevator in the Manitoba inspection division or in an eastern transfer elevator, shall gr in of different grades be mixed together while in store.
Provision is also made to prevent the mixing of grain. Also in the Inspection and Sale Act, section 9, there is a provision that the inspector is to have control of the storage and shipping of grain, and shall keep proper records of all grain received into store in any terminal elevator, and the Act prevents the transfer of grain from one bin to another. Then it enumerates the powers which the inspector has with respect to the cleaning of grain in these elevators. So that the provisions of the Act passed last year, if enforced by proper and capable government inspectors would ensure just as good preservation of the grain at these terminals and give just

as much satisfaction as any system of government ownership.
Let me point out that every one in western Canada is not in favour of government ownership of terminal elevators. I do not believe that there is any great agitation among the farmers in that respect, although there is for the government ownership of elevators in the interior. I have yet, however, to find that there is any serious agitation for the government ownership of terminal and transfer elevators. I have here two or three opinions from western men on this very point to which I would like to refer. I have, for instance, the opinion of Mr. John Millar, who was chairman of the Grain Commission, and which opinion he expressed at the grain growers' convention at Weyburn on the 20th of February last:
The weights both in and out of the terminal elevators had been found to be satisfactory, but the grain going out seemed to contain rather too much extraneous matter as some of the cleaners were not of the best. It was pointed out that there was a tendency for the elevators to go into the hands of private companies who were themselves handling grain and the report of the commission had recommended that these and the transfer elevators farther east should be .placed under strict government control. This had been done and he believed the producer now had as much protection as government ownership would give him.
I also have here an opinion on the present situation from the Hon. D. W. R. Motherwell, Minister of Agriculture in Saskatchewan :
The government control secured over these elevators by amendment to the Grain Act last session by the federal parliament has given the producer practically every safeguard and security in the way of control which government ownership could possibly give.
There are just one or two points to which I shall refer briefly before taking my seat. There were certain arguments in favour of government ownership advanced at the grain growers' convention at Weyburn, which were practically the same as those put forward to-day by the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Schaffner). The first was that government supervision and control is objectionable because you cannot have proper supervision or effective control. But 1 reply that you would have proper supervision and effective control if the system were properly enforced, as I believe it will be if reasonable time be given the government to work it out.
The next objection is that the warehousemen should have no interest in manipulating the commodity he stores. In that opinion I agree, but I do not agree that to eliminate that interest we require to go the length of government ownership. We can put through legislation which will just as Mr. W. M. MARTIN.
effectively accomplish the same object. Another objection is that manipulation was going on at the terminal elevators before the last change in the Manitoba Act respecting the supervision of binning and is going on still. Well, no evidence has been produced to-night to show that manipulation is going on to-day. I may believe that it is, but before supporting such a radical measure as government ownership, I would require some evidence that these abuses were going on. These are the main objections raised to the present system of government control. At that convention there were many men who were in favour of government ownership of the interior elevators, but no one expressed himself regarding government ownership of terminal elevators to any extent. However the points to which I wish to refer briefly are these. It is said, and I believe truly, that there is a serious shortage in grain shipments going from Fort William and Port Arthur to eastern points, such as Owen Sound and Buffalo and others. It is said that the average shortage during the year 1908, after the grain was weighed by government inspectors, was 44 lbs. per 1,000 bushels from Fort William and Port Arthur as compared with 15 lbs. per 1,000 bushels from Chicago and 10 lbs. per 1,000 bushels from Duluth, and that the total shortage in shipments from these elevators at Fort William and Port Arthur this year amounts to 50,000 bushels. At present the men who ship that grain hold the vessel owners responsible, but the vessel owners claim they should not be responsible, although legally they are, owing to the manner in which the grain is weighed. That surely is a hardship to the vessel owners. I was present at a conference before the Minister of Trade and Commerce, in which the vessel owners, shippers, and grain men from Winnipeg appeared, and all agreed that this grain shortage must be m those elevators at Fort William and Port Arthur. Well, if these elevator companies are getting that 50,000 bushels, they are getting what they are not entitled to. According to the Manitoba Grain Act ^ and its amendments last year, they are entitled to a certain amount for binning and a certain amount for storage, but if they are getting that 50,000 bushels they are getting what does not belong to them. Some amendment should be introduced into the Manitoba Grain Act to provide that the surplus be taken over by the government and thus eliminate the question of personal gain. Another matter is that of screening. Before the inspector in Winnipeg grades a car of grain, he marks it so much dockage, sometimes two per cent, and sometimes more and sometimes less. The grain goes into

the elevators at Fort William and Port Arthur, and is supposed to be cleaned to whatever percentage of dockage was set. The elevator men get the screenings. I have heard the amount estimated last year all the way from 300,000 bushels to 1,400,000 bushels. On these screenings the farmers of the west have to pay freight, and they should not belong to the'elevator men, but should go to the producer or at least, the producer should be re-imbursed for his outlay in freight for what at present he gets no return. It is of course to the advantage of the warehouse men to take every possible bushel of screenings they can get. I am advised that they sold the screenings last year to one firm at $7 per ton and that firm retailed it at $16 per ton. But take the price at $7 a ton, and on 300,000 bushels, that amounted to $63,000. On 1,400,000 bushels, it would be five times that sum. Some legislation should be passed to the effect that the surplus screenings and grain found in the elevators at any time shall be confiscated and taken over by the government and thus you will eliminate the element of illegitimate gain which these elevators are getting at present.
I desire to refer in closing to what the Inspection and Sales Act provides with respect to the surplus of grain in the terminals. Subsection 7 of sec. 9 of chapter 36 of the Inspection and Sales Act of 1908 says that:
In the month of August in each year stock shall he taken of the quantity of each grade grain in the terminal elevators.
Why do not. they go a step further and say that the grain and the screenings found there shall belong to the government? I believe that these difficulties could be removed by these suggestions, and I hope that at some future day legislation of this kind will be introduced into this House. A very simple amendment would effect it, and I think it would cure a great majority of objections raised to the handling of grain in these elevators. I am as much interested as are the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Schaffner) and others from the west in seeing that a proper system is devised for handling the grain of our western	provinces.
I am interested in seeing that the producer, no matter how small a producer he may be, gets as much as the market will allow him at the time of sale. I am as much interested as these hon. gentlemen in seeing that no discrimination shall exist between small shippers and large shippers, or, if there is to be an advantage, that it shall be to the small shipper. I believe in the system of government control of these utilities, but I do not believe in the government going aside from its true duty and engaging in mercantile business. I believe that, at least, the government should 127
try in every way to regulate the grain trade of the west before they embark upon the management of terminal elevators and become grain men. As that is my belief, I will move an amendment to that effect, and in doing so I have every confidence that this government-which has been in power since 1896 and under which the Manitoba Grain Act has come into existence and under which the farmers of the west have the right to get cars and ship their own grain-if government control does not prove effective, will be ready to adopt such measures as they deem necessary from time to time to protect the grain interests of .western Canada. The amendment I move is as follows:
That all the words after ' that' be struck cut, and the following be substituted therefor:
The amendments of last session to the Grain Act whereby all transfer and terminal elevators were put under government oontrol have produced good results. Aud if, on further experience, it is found that the present system of supervision is not adequate to prevent the undue mixture of grain in such elevators, this House will be prepared to accept such further legislation as may be needed to that end.
In conclusion, I wish to refer to the fact that since September 1, 1908, only one complaint has been received by the Department of Trade and Commerce from men purchasing grain shipped through these elevators, anl this in contrast with the fact that many such complaints were received in former years. The complaint referred to was from t!ie Dominion Millers' Association, and I have here a short extract from that complaint. It will be observed that they go so far as to admit that there has been an improvement in the handling of the grain in these elevators, although they state it is not yet all it should be.
While there has been a oertain improvement in the grain as it comes from the public elevators at Fort William and Port Arthur since the government took closer control, yet we regret to say that matteis are not yet in a satisfactory condition.
If, under the present system, after it has been in existence but a few months the condition of things is better than before, there is every reason to believe that it will still further improve, especially when the system itself is improved as experience may indicate to be necessary.
Do I understand the amendment to say that the terminal elevators were put under government control?

all transfer and terminal elevators were
put under government control
That is not the case.

Mr Speaker, I should not attempt to speak at any length either on this motion or on the amendment, but I wish to put myself on record so that the people of the west may know where I stand on this very important question. I am glad that the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Schaffner) has introduced this motion. I believe that no motion has ever been introduced into this House, no discussion has ever taken place in the House, of greater importance and interest to the farmers of the western prairies than this. I am much surprised at the hon. member for Regina (Mr. W. M. Martin) stating that the terminal elevators are now under government control. This is the first time I have heard such a statement made. I have always understood that there were government inspectors to supervise the taking in and shipping out of the grain, but so far as general government control is concerned, the idea is entirely new to me. The principal argument put forward by the hon. member on the other side against the government taking actual control of the terminal and transfer elevators seems to be that vested rights stand in the way. Well, I do not know what this House may think of that, but my personal opinion is that, if private corporations invest money in terminal elevators and they are not doing what is honest and just by the farmers, the government is perfectly justified in taking control, or in expropriating, or going into competition with them. And it is the general opinion of the western farmers that they are not getting justice in the terminal elevators. I have not had much experience in the handling of grain myself, and do not pretend to be an authority on the subject, but those from the west who were in the House a year ago, and who took a deep interest in the matter, know what went on before the Department of Trade and Commerce when representations were made by the delegation sent here from the Western Farmers' Associations. That delegation consisted of members from each of the provinces appointed by the different associations, and represented the entire grain growing interest of the three prairie provinces. No one could listen to their arguments without coming to the conclusion that it would be of great advantage to the western grain growers if the government would take over these elevators and control and operate them. I might suggest that, if vested rights are going to be a great obstacle in the way of taking control of the elevators at Port Arthur and Fort William and the transfer elevators further east, the government will have an opportunity to ex-Mr. SCHAFFNER.
periment on the Pacific coast. I understand that meetings have been held in Alberta and Saskatchewan recently which have taken up the question of shipping grain to Europe by the Pacific coast. There are no elevators there as yet, so there will be an opportunity for the government to step in and experiment with government-owned elevators. -From what I have heard from the farmers who laid the case before the' Minister of Trade and Commerce representing the government, I am led to believe that, if the government could see their way clear to take over these existing terminal elevators, they would be rendering one of the greatest services ever rendered to the farmers of the western country. They talk about one or two cents a bushel being taken from the farmers by the manipulation of wheat in these elevators. I have heard it stated that in many cases they take as high as seven cents a bushel from the farmers, at least the farmers think so, I do not know whether that is the case or not.
Does the hon. gentleman refer to the terminal elevators?

Yes, that they are making an undue charge at the terminal elevators at Port Arthur and Fort William; in -fact it is claimed that they are making almost double the charge they should make, at the terminal elevators in particular. The grain pays for all this. This House need not think that if the government take the action suggested by the resolution they would have to pay the expense, because the country would not be out by it. The grain is going to pay for all the handling, and even if the government did step in and operate the elevators five years as an experiment, no doubt some arrangement could be made by which the government would not be out a cent of money. I think this resolution is a step in the right direction, and I sincerely hope the government will accept it, and make an experiment of controlling and operating the terminal and other elevators on the great lakes.
As the hour is late, I beg to move the adjournment of the debate.
Motion agreed to, and debate adjourned.
